periods.title: Uttar Pradesh — Complete History Flow & Timeline
periods.tagline: For UPPSC (Prelims + Mains) — GS Paper I & II — The Land of Lord Ram, Lord Krishna, Buddha & Mahavira
periods.overview: A master flow chart of Uttar Pradesh's entire history, from prehistoric settlements through the Vedic, Mahajanapada, Mauryan, Gupta, Harsha, Gurjara-Pratihara, Chandella/Kalachuri, Gahadavala, Delhi Sultanate, Jaunpur Sultanate, Mughal and Later Mughal periods, to the Revolt of 1857, British rule, socio-religious reform movements, and the formation of the modern state of Uttar Pradesh in 1950. Each phase below is explored in full depth on its own dedicated page.

phases.name: Ancient Age
points: Prehistoric & early settlements (before 1500 BCE); Vedic Period (1500–600 BCE) — Kuru, Panchal, Kashi, Kosala, Videha

Mahajanapadas (600–322 BCE) — 16 Mahajanapadas, capital Shravasti, Kashi, Kaushambi; Maurya Period (322–185 BCE) — Chandragupta Maurya from Pippalivana (near Gorakhpur), Ashoka's edicts in Kaushambi, Sarnath
Post-Maurya Period (185 BCE–320 CE) — Shunga, Kanva, Indo-Greeks, Kushanas; Gupta Period (320–647 CE) — Golden Age of India, Allahabad Pillar Inscription (Samudragupta)

phases.name: Early Medieval Age
points: Harsha Period (606–647 CE) — capital Kannauj, visited by Xuanzang; Gurjara-Pratiharas (730–1036 CE) — capital Kannauj, struggle with Palas & Rashtrakutas
Kalachuris & Chandellas (9th–12th century) — Khajuraho temples (cultural glory); Gahadavalas (11th–12th century) — capital Kannauj & Varanasi, decline due to invasions
Foundation of Cities — Varanasi, Prayagraj, Kannauj flourish; temples, mathas and education centres develop

phases.name: Medieval Age
points: Delhi Sultanate Period (1206–1398) — Qutb-ud-din Aibak, Iltutmish, Balban, many battles in the Doab region; Sayyid & Lodi Dynasty (1398–1526) — control from Delhi, Sikandar Lodi developed Agra, Jaunpur

Jaunpur Sultanate (1394–1479) — Sharqi Dynasty, capital Jaunpur, known for architecture (Atala Masjid); Mughal Period (1526–1707) — Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi (First Battle of Panipat 1526), Akbar developed Agra, Fatehpur Sikri, Allahabad
Later Mughals (1707–1857) — decline of Mughal Empire, Rohillas, Nawabs, and Marathas gain influence

phases.name: Modern Age
points: Revolt of 1857 — major centres Meerut, Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi, Azamgarh; leaders Nana Saheb, Begum Hazrat Mahal, Kunwar Singh
British Rule & Administration — establishment of North-Western Provinces (later United Provinces); development of railways, roads, education; land revenue systems (Zamindari, Talukdari)
Socio-Religious Movements — Arya Samaj (Swami Dayanand), Aligarh Movement (Sir Syed Ahmad Khan), Ramakrishna Mission, Theosophical Society influence

Freedom Struggle in U.P. — Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Quit India Movements; key leaders Pt. Nehru, Purushottam Das Tandon, Govind Ballabh Pant; United Provinces was a major political unit under British India

phases.name: Post Independence
points: Formation of U.P. — U.P. Act, 1950; came into existence on 24 January 1950; capital Lucknow
Reorganization — 9 November 2000: carved out Uttarakhand (then Uttaranchal); present U.P. boundaries established
Political Developments — 1950–1967: Congress rule; 1967 onwards: coalition era; 2017 onwards: new political dynamic

Economic & Social Progress — Green Revolution in Western U.P.; industrial development (Noida, Kanpur, Lucknow, Ghaziabad); schemes: Purvanchal Development, Smart Cities; U.P. is the most populous state of India, with major cultural, spiritual, economic and political importance

Why Important for UPPSC: U.P. has a rich historical, cultural, religious and political heritage; many MCQs and Descriptive questions come from U.P. history
Key for General Studies Paper I & II, Essay, and Interview
Ayodhya — birthplace of Lord Ram; Kashi (Varanasi) — spiritual capital; Prayagraj — Sangam, Kumbh Mela; Sarnath — Buddha's first sermon
Shravasti — Lord Buddha's stay; Kaushambi — Buddhist site; Mathura — Lord Krishna's birthplace; Agra — Taj Mahal, Fatehpur Sikri; Jhansi — Rani Lakshmibai; Lucknow — Nawabi culture & capital
Important Personalities: Gautam Buddha, Mahavira, Chandragupta Maurya, Ashoka, Harshavardhana, Raja Suheldev, Alauddin Khalji, Akbar, Begum Hazrat Mahal, Nana Saheb, Govind Ballabh Pant

events.title: 16 Mahajanapadas in the Ganga-Yamuna Doab
events.desc: Kashi, Kosala, Vatsa, Kuru, Panchala and Surasena — six of the sixteen Mahajanapadas — are centred in present-day Uttar Pradesh.

events.title: Uttar Pradesh comes into existence
events.desc: The United Provinces are renamed Uttar Pradesh under the U.P. Act, 1950, with Lucknow as its capital.

events.title: Uttarakhand carved out
events.desc: The hill districts of Uttar Pradesh are separated to form the new state of Uttarakhand (initially Uttaranchal).

prelims: Focus on U.P.-specific facts; learn important dynasties and kings; remember important places & their significance
Link events with All-India history; make short notes & timelines; solve PYQs
mains: U.P. is important for GS Paper I (History & Culture) & GS Paper II; essay and interview questions often draw on U.P.'s civilisational role
Trace the continuous thread from the Vedic Janapadas through the Mahajanapadas, Mauryas, Guptas, and medieval sultanates to the freedom struggle and the formation of the modern state

quickFacts: Birthplace of Lord Ram (Ayodhya), Lord Krishna (Mathura), and home to Buddhism's and Jainism's earliest sites

periods.title: Prehistoric & Early Settlements of Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: From Earliest Times to 1500 BCE (Before the Vedic Period) — U.P. in the Cradle of Indian Civilization
periods.overview: Uttar Pradesh has one of the longest cultural sequences in India, moving through the Old Stone Age, Mesolithic, Neolithic, and Chalcolithic/Early Settlement phases before the arrival of Vedic culture around 1500 BCE. Key sites like Belan Valley, Lahuradewa (among the earliest known rice-cultivation sites in South Asia), Sarai Nahar Rai, Chopani-Mando, Mahagara, Narhan and Atranjikhera trace the journey from nomadic hunter-gatherer bands to settled, agricultural, and eventually early urban communities.

phases.name: Old Stone Age (Palaeolithic)
points: Early humans, hunting and food gathering; use of crude stone tools; nomadic life

phases.name: Mesolithic Age
points: Microlithic tools; hunting, fishing, food gathering; rock shelters & cave habitations

phases.name: Neolithic Age
points: Neolithic (polished) tools; agriculture begins; domestication of animals; semi-settled life

phases.name: Early Settlements / Chalcolithic
points: Copper tools and pottery; permanent settlements; trade & exchange; early social & cultural development

phases.name: Transition to Vedic Period
points: Aryan settlements begin in Western U.P.; transition from the prehistoric to the historical age

Life & Culture by Phase: Old Stone Age: nomadic life, hunting/fishing/food gathering, hand axes/cleavers/choppers, caves & rock shelters, small bands based on family groups, animism

Mesolithic Age: semi-nomadic, microlithic tools (blades, points, scrapers), bow & arrow, rock shelters/seasonal camps, clan-based groups, spirit worship & early Mother Goddess worship, rock paintings (Chopani-Mando)

Neolithic Age: settled life begins, agriculture (rice, wheat, barley), domestication of cattle/buffalo/goat/dog, mud huts, polished stone tools (axes, adzes), headman as early form of leader, worship of Mother Goddess & fertility cult

Chalcolithic/Early Settlements: permanent villages, planned rectangular houses, copper tools alongside stone tools, surplus production & barter trade, growth of villages and division of labour, mother goddess idols and terracotta figurines
Important Archaeological Sites: Belan Valley (Mirzapur, Sonbhadra) — one of the earliest human habitations in India, Acheulian tools found
Chopani-Mando (Pratapgarh) — Mesolithic rock shelter, microlithic tools, animal drawings
Mahagara (Rae Bareli) — Neolithic-Chalcolithic site, pottery, stone tools, house remains, agriculture evidence
Sarai Nahar Rai (Baghpat) — Chalcolithic settlement (2600–1900 BCE), copper objects, pottery, beads, remains of huts
Lahuradewa (Sant Kabir Nagar) — one of the earliest known agricultural sites in India (7000–2000 BCE), rice cultivation evidence
Narhan (Ballia) — Chalcolithic culture, Painted Grey Ware (later stage), early farming community
Atranjikhera (Etah) — early urban settlement (2nd millennium BCE), beads, seals, terracotta figurines
Contribution of Men & Women: Men: hunting & protection of the group, making tools & weapons, clearing land for agriculture, construction of huts, trade & exchange, leadership roles

Women: collection of fruits/roots/seeds, early agriculture (sowing, weeding, harvesting), pottery making, care of children & elderly, domestication of animals, making ornaments & handicrafts; both men and women contributed equally to the development of society and culture

events.title: Rice cultivation at Lahuradewa
events.desc: One of the earliest known agricultural sites in South Asia, providing key evidence for the origins of settled farming in the region.

events.title: Transition to the Vedic Age begins
events.desc: Aryan settlements appear in Western U.P., marking the transition from prehistory to the historical Vedic period.

prelims: U.P. has one of the longest cultural sequences in India; Belan Valley is one of the earliest human habitats; Lahuradewa is the earliest evidence of rice cultivation in India
mains: Discuss the archaeological significance of Lahuradewa; describe important Chalcolithic sites in U.P.; write about the contribution of women in early societies
Transition from nomadic to settled, agricultural, urban life laid the foundation for later Vedic, Mahajanapada and historic civilizations

quickFacts: Belan Valley (Mirzapur, Sonbhadra) — earliest human habitation
Vedic Age begins in Western U.P., c. 1500 BCE

periods.title: Vedic Age in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: The Evolution of Vedic Culture in the Land of Ganga-Yamuna Doab
periods.overview: As Aryan tribes moved east from the Sapta-Sindhu region into the Ganga-Yamuna Doab, Uttar Pradesh became the cultural heartland of the Vedic Age. Through the Early, Later, Late/Upanishadic and Transition phases, the region saw the rise of the Janas of Kuru, Panchala, Kashi, Kosala and Surasena — the seedbed from which the Mahajanapadas would later emerge.

phases.name: Early Vedic
points: Aryans enter the Sapta-Sindhu region and gradually move east; in U.P., they settle along the Ganga-Yamuna Doab; cattle rearing, simple agriculture, clan-based life

phases.name: Later Vedic
points: Expansion across U.P. plains; permanent settlements established; rise of Janas and early states; development of agriculture, irrigation and trade

phases.name: Late Vedic / Upanishadic
points: Rise of Kuru-Panchala culture in western U.P.; growth of learning and philosophy (Upanishads); social & political systems become more complex

phases.name: Transition to Mahajanapadas
points: Janapadas emerge: Kuru, Panchala, Kashi, Kosala, Surasena; urbanization, trade & crafts grow; society moves towards the Mahajanapada era

Society, Polity & Economy by Phase: Early Vedic: tribal (Jana) based society, no rigid hierarchy; Gana (clan) based polity, King (Rajan) elected; cattle rearing main occupation; nature worship (Indra, Agni, Varuna)

Later Vedic: Varna system develops, families become patriarchal; monarchy becomes hereditary; agriculture (plough used), surplus production, trade & craft development; more rituals and Yajnas, gods like Prajapati/Vishnu/Rudra

Late Vedic/Upanishadic: caste system becomes stronger, joint family system; Janapadas more organized, kings powerful, taxation begins; iron tools used, trade routes active; rise of philosophy & Upanishads

Transition: society complex, emergence of urban class; formation of Janapadas — Kuru, Panchala, Kosala, Kashi; trade & commerce grow, coinage (punch-marked) begins; rise of Shramana traditions (Buddhism, Jainism later)
Kuru (1500–600 BCE): capital Hastinapur; powerful tribe, Rigvedic & later Vedic importance
Panchala (1500–600 BCE): capital Ahichchhatra, North & South Panchala; centre of learning & culture
Kashi (1500–600 BCE): capital Varanasi; ancient settlement on Ganga, trade & culture centre
Kosala (1000–600 BCE): capital Ayodhya; powerful kingdom on Sarayu, important in the Later Vedic age
Surasena (800–600 BCE): capital Mathura; Yadu tribe, trade & cultural importance
Important Vedic Literature Composed: Rigveda — early Vedic hymns (1500–1200 BCE); Samaveda, Yajurveda, Atharvaveda — later Vedic composition; Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Upanishads (700–500 BCE); Vedangas — phonetics, grammar, astronomy

women.name: Gargi Vachaknavi
women.note: Debated in Brahmavadini gatherings; associated with the region's philosophical tradition.

women.name: Maitreyi
women.note: Seeker of knowledge; wife of Yajnavalkya.

women.name: Lopamudra
women.note: Composer of Rigvedic hymns.

women.name: Apala
women.note: Rigvedic seer.

women.name: Ghosha
women.note: Vedic hymn composer.

events.title: Rigveda composed
events.desc: As Aryan tribes settle in the Sapta-Sindhu region and begin moving toward the Ganga-Yamuna Doab, the earliest Vedic hymns are composed.

events.title: Settlement of the Ganga-Yamuna Doab
events.desc: Later Vedic tribes establish permanent settlements across the plains of Uttar Pradesh, laying the ground for the Janapadas.

events.title: Formation of Janapadas
events.desc: Kuru, Panchala, Kashi, Kosala and Surasena emerge as organized Janapadas, setting the stage for the Mahajanapada age.

people.name: Maharishi Vashishtha
people.note: Mentor of kings.

people.name: Yajnavalkya
people.note: Associated with the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.

people.name: Bharata (of Kurus)
people.note: After whom 'Bharatvarsha' is named, per tradition.

prelims: Ganga-Yamuna Doab became the cultural heartland of Vedic civilization; frequently asked in Prelims & Mains for Art & Culture, Polity, Society, Economy & Religion
mains: Trace the development of the Varna system and family institutions across the Vedic phases in U.P.; this period is the base for understanding later Mahajanapada and Mauryan history
Sites in U.P. are important for the Archaeology section of UPPSC

periods.title: Mahajanapadas of Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Complete Flow, Map & Timeline — U.P. at the Heart of the Mahajanapada Age
periods.overview: Of the sixteen Mahajanapadas of ancient India, six — Kashi, Kosala, Vatsa, Panchala, Kuru and Surasena — were centred in or closely associated with present-day Uttar Pradesh, making the region one of the principal political, economic and cultural theatres of the age. The chapter traces the shift from tribal Janapadas to territorial Mahajanapadas, the rise of Magadhan power, and the eventual foundation of the Mauryan Empire.

phases.name: Later Vedic Transformation
points: From tribal life to settled agriculture; iron use; surplus production

phases.name: Rise of Janapadas
points: Political-territorial units emerge

phases.name: Rise of Mahajanapadas
points: 16 Mahajanapadas emerge across North India

phases.name: Urbanization & Religious Movements
points: Growth of towns and trade; Buddhism, Jainism and Shramana traditions spread

phases.name: Increasing Magadhan Power
points: Bimbisara and Ajatashatru expand Magadha

phases.name: Nanda Expansion & Mauryan Empire
points: Nanda expansion (large empire, centralized rule); Mauryan Empire founded (322 BCE) by Chandragupta Maurya

The 16 Mahajanapadas and Their Link to U: Directly associated with present-day U.P.: Kashi (capital Varanasi), Kosala (capital Shravasti), Vatsa (capital Kaushambi), Kuru (capital Hastinapura), Panchala (capital Ahichchhatra/Kampilya), Surasena (capital Mathura)

Malla (capital Kushinagara/Pava) is partly associated with U.P./Bihar; the remaining Mahajanapadas (Anga, Magadha, Avanti, Chedi, Matsya, Vajji, Gandhara, Kamboja, Assaka) lay outside present-day U.P.
Polity & Governance: Evolution of political form: Tribe/Jana → Janapada → Territorial State → Mahajanapada
Monarchical states: hereditary kingship, king as political & military authority, ministers & officials, tax collection, army, fortified cities (examples: Kosala, Kashi, Vatsa, Surasena)
Gana-Sangha/Republican traditions: collective leadership, assemblies (Sabha, Sanstha), clan-based participation, oligarchic system (important in wider U.P. region, e.g. Malla of Kushinagara, Pava)
Society & Economy: Evolution of society: Clan-based → Territorial → Urban society; Varna system becomes more structured; emergence of occupational specialization (farmers, artisans, merchants, traders, officials, rulers)

Economic features: agriculture as the main occupation, iron tools increase productivity, surplus production; craft production (pottery, metalwork, textiles, bead making); trade & commerce (local and long distance); use of punch-marked coins; growth of towns and urban centres; banking and credit in early forms
Role & Contribution of Men and Women: Men: political & military roles (kings, warriors, ministers, administrators, fortification builders); economic roles (farmers, artisans, merchants, caravan traders, metalworkers, potters); intellectual & religious roles (Brahmins, teachers/acharyas, philosophers, monks)

Women: participated in household and economic production; elite women could influence political & dynastic relationships; participated in religious & intellectual traditions; Buddhist and Jain traditions welcomed women (Bhikkhuni Sangha, Jain Sadhvis); some women known for learning, wisdom & philosophical dialogues (Gargi, Maitreyi in tradition); property rights were limited but not entirely absent

women.name: Women in the Mahajanapada Age
women.note: Participated in household & economic production; some elite women influenced political and dynastic relationships and engaged in religious and philosophical traditions, though sources are limited and regional variations existed.

events.title: Formation of the 16 Mahajanapadas
events.desc: Territorial states with defined capitals emerge across North India, six of them centred in present-day U.P.

events.title: Rise of Magadhan power
events.desc: Bimbisara and Ajatashatru expand Magadha's influence, eventually eclipsing many U.P.-based Mahajanapadas.

events.title: Foundation of the Mauryan Empire
events.desc: Chandragupta Maurya establishes the Mauryan Empire, absorbing the Mahajanapadas of the Gangetic plains including those in present-day U.P.

people.name: Prasenajit
people.note: A prominent Mahajanapada ruler based at Shravasti.

people.name: Udayana
people.note: Based at Kaushambi.

people.name: Gautama Buddha
people.note: Active across the Mahajanapadas of the region.

people.name: Mahavira
people.note: Associated with the wider Mahajanapada world.

prelims: Kashi, Kosala, Vatsa, Panchala, Kuru, Surasena — the six Mahajanapadas associated with present-day Uttar Pradesh; do not equate ancient Gana-Sanghas directly with modern democracy
mains: Uttar Pradesh was at the heart of the Mahajanapada age — politically vibrant, economically active and culturally dynamic; master the flow, map and polity for UPPSC success

quickFacts: Kashi, Kosala, Vatsa, Kuru, Panchala, Surasena
Varanasi, Shravasti, Kaushambi, Hastinapura, Ahichchhatra/Kampilya, Mathura
Absorption into the Mauryan Empire, 322 BCE

periods.title: Maurya Period in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Complete Study Chart — U.P. as a Core Part of the Mauryan Empire
periods.overview: Uttar Pradesh formed a core, strongly-integrated part of the Mauryan Empire, organized under the provinces of Kosala, Kashi, Panchala, Vatsa and Surasena. Ashoka's reign left a particularly deep imprint on the region through inscriptions, stupas and Dhamma-based administration at sites like Sarnath, Kaushambi and Prayagraj.

phases.name: Chandragupta Maurya
points: Establishes the Mauryan Empire; Pataliputra (Magadha) capital; Uttar Pradesh integrated into a unified empire

phases.name: Bindusara
points: Extends the empire further south and west

phases.name: Ashoka the Great
points: Kalinga War (c. 261 BCE); embraces Dhamma; intensive administrative, economic and religious developments in U.P.

phases.name: Post-Ashoka
points: Gradual decline, rise of provincial governors' autonomy

phases.name: End of the Mauryas
points: Last Maurya ruler Brihadratha killed by his general Pushyamitra Shunga

Maurya Administration & Important Centre: Ahichchhatra (Panchala region) — important Mauryan administrative & military centre; Shravasti (Kosala) — provincial capital during Mauryan rule; Hastinapura (Kuru region) — Mauryan presence, part of the northern provincial system

Kampilya (Panchala) — Mauryan control over Panchala territory; Sarnath (near Varanasi) — where the Buddha delivered the Dhammachakra Pravartana, major Buddhist centre especially under Ashoka; Varanasi (Kashi) — important city, trade & craft centre under the Mauryas; Kaushambi (Vatsa region) — important urban & administrative centre on the Yamuna; Prayagraj (ancient Prayaga) — confluence (Triveni), important religious/economic/strategic centre; Mathura (Surasena region) — major urban centre, trade & religion (Mauryan sculptures, Yakshi, inscriptions)
Maurya Administrative System (Arthashast: King (Chakravartin) at the apex; Mantri Parishad (council of ministers), Yuvaraja, Mahamatras (high officials), Kumara/Aryaputra (provincial governors)

Important officials: Samaharta (revenue collection), Sannidhata (treasury officer), Dandanayaka (military chief), Nagarak (city superintendent), Pautavadhyaksha (weights & measures), Dharma Mahamatras (moral welfare)
U.P. was divided into Pradeshas (provinces) and Ahara/Vishayas (districts); strong central administration with a network of officers; use of spies/secret agents (gudhapurusha)
Agriculture: well-developed irrigation, use of plough and seeds; trade & commerce: active trade on Ganga-Yamuna routes; industry & crafts: textiles, pottery, metalwork, ivory, beads, stone craft; state control over mines, forests, salt, liquor; punch-marked coins in circulation
Public Works & Ashoka's Dhamma: Construction of roads, bridges, rest houses; tree plantation, wells, tanks; ferries and boating facilities; fortified towns

After the Kalinga War, Ashoka adopted Dhamma — promoting non-violence, compassion, respect for all sects; inscriptions and edicts spread across U.P.; support to Buddhism while respecting other religions; establishment of stupas, viharas, pillars; Dhamma-Mahamatras appointed for moral upliftment
Polished Mauryan pillars; Sarnath Lion Capital; Yakshi sculptures (Mathura); Barabar-style influence on cave architecture; stupas & monasteries at Sarnath, Kaushambi

events.title: U.P. integrated into the Mauryan Empire
events.desc: Chandragupta Maurya's establishment of the empire brings the region's former Mahajanapadas under unified Mauryan rule.

events.title: Ashoka's edicts appear across U.P.
events.desc: Following the Kalinga War, Ashoka's Dhamma-based inscriptions and edicts spread across Mauryan U.P., especially at Kaushambi and Sarnath.

events.title: End of Mauryan rule
events.desc: Pushyamitra Shunga assassinates the last Mauryan ruler, ending Mauryan control over the region.

people.name: Chandragupta Maurya
people.note: Integrated U.P. into a unified empire.

people.name: Ashoka the Great
people.note: Left the deepest imprint on U.P. through Dhamma and inscriptions.

people.name: Kumara Mahendra
people.note: Sent to Sri Lanka for Buddhism, per tradition.

people.name: Chanakya
people.note: All-India Mauryan figure.

prelims: U.P. was a core part of the Mauryan Empire; important centres — Sarnath, Kaushambi, Shravasti, Ahichchhatra, Mathura, Prayagraj, Varanasi
mains: Connect Mauryan sites in U.P. with administration, economy and religion for better answers; Ashoka's Dhamma and administrative measures had a deep impact on U.P.

quickFacts: Regions of Maurya Administration in U.P.
Administrative practices, urban centres and spread of Buddhism continued after Mauryan decline

periods.title: Post-Maurya Period in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: From the Decline of the Mauryas to the Rise of the Gupta Empire in North India
periods.overview: After the Mauryan decline, Uttar Pradesh passed through the hands of the Shungas, Kanvas, Indo-Greeks, Indo-Scythians (Shakas), Indo-Parthians, Kushanas and various early local dynasties (Nagas, Yaudheyas, Kunindas) before Gupta power began expanding into the region from Magadha around 320 CE. Despite political diversity, the period saw cultural unity, growth of trade, and the flourishing of Buddhism, Jainism and Brahmanism side by side, especially in the Mathura region.

phases.name: Shunga & Kanva Influence
points: Decline of the Mauryas; Pushyamitra Shunga establishes the Shunga Dynasty (185–73 BCE), influence extended in eastern U.P. including Prayagraj; Kanva Dynasty (73–28 BCE) ruled from Pataliputra, controlled parts of eastern U.P.

phases.name: Indo-Greek & Indo-Scythian Influence
points: Rise of local powers, Indo-Greek, Indo-Scythian (Shaka), Indo-Parthian and early Kushanas; western U.P. (Mathura, Saketa, Panchala region) under their influence

phases.name: Kushana Power
points: Kushanas become a major power in U.P. (1st–3rd century CE); important centres: Mathura (capital of Kushana Satraps), Saketa, Kaushambi, Varanasi; growth of urban centres, trade, Buddhism, Jainism, Brahmanism

phases.name: Rise of Gupta Power
points: From c. 320 CE, Gupta power expands from Magadha into the U.P. region, ending the Post-Mauryan phase

Major Dynasties / Powers (185 BCE – 320: Shunga (185–73 BCE): capital Pataliputra; rise of Brahmanical traditions, Buddhist patronage continued
Kanva (73–28 BCE): capital Pataliputra; continuation of Shunga policies, gradual decline
Indo-Greek (c. 2nd–1st century BCE): capital Saketa/Mathura; Greek rulers, bilingual coins, trade & culture exchange
Indo-Scythian/Shaka (1st century BCE–1st century CE): Mathura region; Kshatrapas ruled, silver coins, rise of trade
Indo-Parthian (1st–2nd century CE): Mathura region; bridged Greeks and Kushanas, issued coins
Kushana (1st–3rd century CE): capital Mathura; major power, great patronage to Buddhism, art & trade
Early Local Dynasties (Nagas, Yaudheyas, Kunindas etc., 1st–3rd century CE): various parts of western U.P.; republican traditions, issue of coins
Polity & Governance: Monarchies: hereditary kingship, king as supreme authority, council of ministers (Mantriparishad), officials (Mahamatras, Amatyas, Senapati), tax collection, maintenance of army & forts, law and order through local officials

Republican traditions: clan-based oligarchic republics, decisions taken in assemblies (Sabhas/Sanghas), headed by chiefs or elected representatives (examples in the wider region: Yaudheyas, Malavas, Arjunayanas, Kunindas, Nagas) — note: republican systems were oligarchic, not democratic in the modern sense
Society & Economy: Varna system continued and became more rigid; Brahmins gained importance; Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras had traditional roles; growth of new social groups — artisans, traders, guilds (Shrenis); urbanisation increased

Agriculture, crafts & industries (pottery, metal, beads, textiles); trade & commerce (caravan, river routes, ports); use of coins (punch-marked, die-struck, gold, silver, copper); guilds (Shrenis) & occupational specialisation; important trade centres — Mathura (international trade hub), Saketa (Ayodhya), Kaushambi, Prayaga, Varanasi
Religious & Cultural Developments: Buddhism: continued patronage under Shungas and Kushanas; monasteries & stupas developed (Sarnath, Kaushambi, Sankisa)
Jainism: flourished; spread of Digambara and Svetambara traditions; Jain monks travelled widely, supported by merchants & urban groups
Brahmanism & Hinduism: revival of Brahmanical traditions under Shungas; construction of temples began; worship of Vishnu, Shiva, Skanda, Devi; development of Puranic traditions
Art & Architecture: Mathura School of Art — red sandstone sculptures, Yaksha-yakshi and Buddha images, Jain Tirthankaras, realistic human figures
Stupas & Monuments — Sarnath, Kaushambi, Sankisa important Buddhist sites; early temple architecture developed; brick & stone structures; Brahmi and Kharoshthi scripts used in inscriptions

events.title: Decline of Mauryas, rise of the Shungas
events.desc: Pusyamitra Shunga establishes the Shunga Dynasty following the fall of the Mauryas.

events.title: Kushana rule centred at Mathura
events.desc: The Kushanas make Mathura a key centre of Buddhist art, trade and patronage.

events.title: Rise of Gupta power
events.desc: Gupta power begins expanding from Magadha into the U.P. region, ending the Post-Mauryan phase.

people.name: Kanishka
people.note: Centred power at Mathura.

prelims: The period (185 BCE–320 CE) was a transition from Mauryan centralized rule to regional kingdoms and early empires; Mathura region was the cultural and artistic heart of the period
mains: Political diversity but cultural unity is the defining feature; Buddhist, Jain and Brahmanical traditions flourished together; this period laid the foundation for the rise of the Gupta Empire

quickFacts: Shunga, Kanva, Indo-Greek, Indo-Scythian, Indo-Parthian, Kushana
Mathura, Saketa, Kaushambi, Prayaga, Varanasi, Sravasti, Ahichchhatra
Brahmi, Kharoshthi / Punch-marked, Silver, Copper, Gold (die-struck)

periods.title: Gupta Period in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Golden Age of India — U.P. as a Core Region of the Gupta Empire
periods.overview: Uttar Pradesh was a core region of the Gupta Empire — politically, economically and culturally. Prayaga (Allahabad), Kashi, Mathura and Kaushambi were major centres, and the Prayagaprasasti (Allahabad Pillar Inscription of Samudragupta) is among the single most important sources for the entire Gupta age.

phases.name: Chandragupta I
points: Rise of Gupta power; consolidates power in Magadha, influence extends to the Prayag region

phases.name: Samudragupta
points: Conquests across North India including U.P. regions (Prayag, Kosala, Panchala etc.); gains titles like 'Prayagaprasasti' (Allahabad Pillar Inscription)

phases.name: Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya)
points: Expansion, prosperity, cultural efflorescence; Ujjain and Pataliputra important centres

phases.name: Kumaragupta I
points: Stability, continuation of administration and cultural progress

phases.name: Skandagupta
points: Defeated the Huns (Pushyamitras) in the North-West, protected the empire including the U.P. region

phases.name: Later Guptas
points: Gradual decline due to succession disputes, Huna pressure and regional assertion

Gupta Rulers and Their Connection with U: Chandragupta I (c. 320–335 CE): Pataliputra; consolidated power in Magadha, influence extended to Prayag region
Samudragupta (c. 335–375 CE): Pataliputra; covered Aryavarta including U.P. regions (Prayag, Kosala, Panchala etc.); described as the 'Napoleon of India'
Chandragupta II Vikramaditya (c. 375–415 CE): Ujjain, Pataliputra; patronized Kashi, Mathura, Sarnath and other centres, strengthened administration; cultural boom, expansion of trade and gold coins
Kumaragupta I (c. 415–455 CE): Pataliputra; continued prosperity in U.P., Mathura art and temples flourished; stable administration, economic growth
Skandagupta (c. 455–467 CE): Pataliputra; defended the empire from Huns (Pushyamitras) in the North-West, protected the U.P. region; military victories, continuity maintained
Administration & Governance: Well-organised centralised administration with provincial and local divisions; King (Maharajadhiraja) at the apex, assisted by Mantri Parishad (council of ministers), Amatyas (high officials), Uparika (provincial governor)

Administrative divisions: Bhukti (province) → Vishaya (district) → Vithi (sub-district) → Grama (village); officials — Uparika, Vishayapati, Dandapashika, Mahadandanayaka, Ayuktas; record keeping, revenue collection and judicial system well developed
Society & Economy: Varna system continued with greater rigidity; Brahmins enjoyed high status and received land grants; growth of towns and urban life; artisans, merchants and traders formed important groups; women enjoyed respect in family & society, some were scholars

Agriculture remained the backbone; use of iron plough, better irrigation, multiple cropping; growth of trade & commerce (internal & external); guilds (shrenis) of traders and artisans flourished; use of gold coins (Dinars) extensively
Religion & Culture: Hinduism (Vaishnavism & Shaivism) was the dominant religion; Buddhism continued with royal patronage (Sarnath, Kushinagar, Kaushambi, Sravasti); Jainism also existed in urban centres; Sanskrit language flourished, classical literature, drama, poetry and epics developed; education centres flourished (Kashi, Mathura, Sarnath); science, mathematics, astronomy, Ayurveda and metallurgy progressed
Land Grants (A Key Feature): Gupta rulers granted land to Brahmins, religious institutions and officials; land grants promoted agriculture, settlement and Sanskritisation; done through copper plate inscriptions (important sites: Sarnath, Damodarpur near Varanasi, Prayag, Rohilkhand region, Mathura region)

events.title: Samudragupta's conquests and the Prayagaprasasti
events.desc: The Allahabad Pillar Inscription, composed by Harisena, records Samudragupta's extensive conquests including regions in present-day U.P.

events.title: Chandragupta II's cultural patronage
events.desc: Kashi, Mathura, and Sarnath flourish culturally under Chandragupta II Vikramaditya's patronage.

events.title: Skandagupta repels the Huns
events.desc: Skandagupta successfully defends the empire, including the U.P. region, against Huna incursions from the North-West.

people.name: Samudragupta
people.note: Called the 'Napoleon of India'; Allahabad Pillar Inscription records his conquests.

people.name: Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya)
people.note: Patron of Kashi, Mathura, Sarnath.

people.name: Kalidasa
people.note: Gem of Sanskrit literature associated with the Gupta court.

people.name: Harisena
people.note: Composed the Prayagaprasasti (Allahabad Pillar Inscription).

prelims: Gupta Empire was at its political and cultural zenith; U.P. was a core region — Prayag, Kashi, Mathura and Kosala were major centres; the Prayagaprasasti is the most important source
mains: Gupta rule gave stability, prosperity, art, literature and religious harmony; foundation of Indian culture, science, art and administration was strengthened during this period

quickFacts: Pataliputra (outside U.P.) / Prayag, Kashi, Mathura, Kaushambi, Sravasti, Ahichchhatra
Culture, Art, Literature, Science — Golden Age of India

periods.title: The Harsha Period in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Golden Age After Gupta — Political Unity, Cultural Flowering, Religious Harmony, Patronage of Learning & Art
periods.overview: Harshavardhana of the Pushyabhuti dynasty made Uttar Pradesh the heartland of his empire, with Kannauj (Kanyakubja) as his later capital and Sthanesvara (Thanesar), Prayaga, Kaushambi, Mathura, Varanasi and Shravasti all playing major roles. His reign, described in detail by the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, represents the last great attempt at political unity in North India before the region fragmented into regional kingdoms.

phases.name: Accession
points: Harsha becomes King of Thanesar after the death of his brother Rajyavardhana

phases.name: Consolidation
points: Establishes control over Punjab, Haryana and parts of Uttar Pradesh

phases.name: Expansion
points: Consolidation of power in Uttar Pradesh and North India; defeats many rulers

phases.name: Conflict with the Chalukyas
points: Conflict with Chalukya king Pulakeshin II; the Narmada River becomes the southern boundary

phases.name: Grand Assembly at Prayaga
points: Grand religious assembly at Prayaga (Allahabad) — distribution of wealth to the people

phases.name: Death of Harsha
points: Death of Harsha at Kanyakubja (Kannauj)

Harsha — The King & His Empire: Belonged to the Pushyabhuti dynasty; succeeded his brother Rajyavardhana; a great conqueror, able administrator and patron of arts, literature and religion

His empire extended over Punjab, Haryana and parts of Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Bengal; the Narmada River formed the southern boundary (following conflict with the Chalukyas); administration was efficient but not as highly centralized as the Mauryas
Administration & Governance: Monarchical rule: Harsha was a benevolent king who exercised personal supervision over administration; territorial division: empire divided into Bhuktis (provinces), further divided into Vishayas (districts) and Patakas (sub-districts)

Officials: Upa-Rajukas, Vishaya-patis, Dandanayakas, Mahattaras and Sresthins were important officials; king was the supreme authority in justice, punishment for crime was moderate; land revenue was the main source, with trade, taxes, fines and tributes as other sources; large standing army with infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots; maintained friendly relations with neighbouring states through embassies
Religion & Culture: Harsha was a great patron of Buddhism, but respected all religions; himself described as a follower of Mahayana Buddhism; supported Brahmanism, Jainism and other sects; grand religious assemblies at Prayaga (c. 643–644 CE) once every five years

Flourishing of Sanskrit literature and learning; Harsha himself was a scholar and playwright; famous works: Nagananda and Ratnavali (dramas), and Priyadarshika (these are among the known works); development of art, sculpture and architecture continued; centres of learning — Nalanda, Valabhi, Kanyakubja, Varanasi and Mathura
Chinese Traveller — Xuanzang (Hsuan Tsan: Xuanzang visited Harsha's court c. 630–645 CE; described Harsha as a kind, generous and religious king; provided a detailed account of cities, administration, society, religion, education and economy of the period; his travelogue 'Si-yu-ki' is a valuable historical source
Decline of Harsha's Empire: No capable successor after Harsha's death in 647 CE; the empire broke into smaller states; rise of regional powers — Gurjara-Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas in the later period; feudal tendencies and land grants led to disintegration

events.title: Harsha becomes King
events.desc: Harsha ascends the throne at Thanesar after his brother Rajyavardhana's death, beginning his reign centred on North India including U.P.

events.title: Grand assembly at Prayaga
events.desc: Harsha holds a grand religious assembly at Prayaga, distributing wealth to the people every five years.

events.title: Xuanzang visits Harsha's court
events.desc: The Chinese pilgrim's detailed travelogue, 'Si-yu-ki', becomes a key historical source on Harsha's India.

events.title: Death of Harsha
events.desc: Harsha dies at Kanyakubja (Kannauj) without a capable successor, leading to the empire's fragmentation.

people.name: Harshavardhana
people.note: r. c. 606–647 CE; made Kannauj his later capital.

people.name: Xuanzang (Hsuan Tsang)
people.note: Visited Harsha's court c. 630–645 CE; authored 'Si-yu-ki'.

people.name: Pulakeshin II
people.note: Defeated Harsha's southward ambitions at the Narmada.

prelims: Harsha's reign marks the last great attempt at political unity in North India before the rise of regional kingdoms; Kanyakubja (Kannauj) was his later capital; Xuanzang's account is a key primary source
mains: Timeline & extent of Harsha's empire; administration and important officials; the grand assembly at Prayaga; Xuanzang's description; religious tolerance & cultural achievements

quickFacts: Kanyakubja, Prayaga, Kaushambi, Varanasi, Mathura, Sravasti, Ahichchhatra

periods.title: Gurjara-Pratiharas in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: The Great Defenders of North India Against Arab Invasions
periods.overview: The Gurjara-Pratiharas, with Kannauj as their imperial capital, played a crucial role in defending North India against Arab invasions from the west, while making Kannauj the greatest imperial and cultural centre in the region and a central prize in the tripartite struggle with the Palas and Rashtrakutas.

phases.name: Rise of Power
points: Rise of Gurjara-Pratihara power in Rajasthan

phases.name: Nagabhata I
points: Emerges as a powerful ruler; defeat of Arab invaders (Muhammad bin Qasim's successors) at Rajasthan, c. 754–756 CE, protecting North India

phases.name: Vatsaraja & Nagabhata II
points: Vatsaraja (775–805 CE) extends territory; Nagabhata II (805–833 CE) defeats Arabs again, extends influence in North India

phases.name: Mihir Bhoja
points: The greatest Pratihara ruler; capital at Kannauj; resisted Palas and Rashtrakutas; patron of literature and art

phases.name: Mahendrapala I & Decline
points: Mahendrapala I (885–915 CE) — last powerful ruler of the early line, empire began to decline after him; 10th–11th century: decline due to internal weakness and rise of Chandellas, Kalachuris, Paramaras

Arab Invasions & the Pratihara Role: Arabs under Muhammad bin Qasim reached Sindh in 712 CE; successors attempted expansion into Rajasthan and western India; Nagabhata I and Nagabhata II defeated Arab forces near Jalore, Bhinmal and the Rajasthan frontiers (c. 754–756 CE)
This saved North India from further Arab expansion and marked the beginning of the Pratiharas' reputation as 'Defenders of North India'
Administration & Governance: Hereditary monarchy with strong central authority; empire divided into Bhuktis (provinces), Vishayas (districts) and Pattakas (sub-districts) and Villages; officials — Uparika (governor), Vishayapati, Dandapashika, Mahattaras, Bhogika and Sresthin (revenue officials)

Revenue system: land revenue as the main source, other taxes — trade tax, profession tax, fines etc.; strong cavalry, elephants and infantry; king supreme in justice, local officers maintained law and order
Society & Economy: Varna system continued; Brahmins enjoyed high status, many land grants; growth of municipalities and urban centres; artisans, traders, merchants and agriculturists contributed to the economy; position of women relatively better in elite families

Agriculture was the backbone of the economy; use of iron plough, irrigation tanks, wells and canals; active trade through land routes (Uttarapatha) and river routes; growth of towns like Kannauj, Mathura, Varanasi, Ahichchhatra, Prayag; guilds (shrenis) of artisans and merchants flourished
Religion & Culture: Patronage to Hinduism — Shaivism, Vaishnavism, Shaktism; maintenance of temples, mathas and tirthas; tolerance towards Buddhism and Jainism continued; many grants to Brahmans and religious institutions

Patronage of Sanskrit literature and scholarship; famous works: Rajatarangini (later period), Harshacharita (Banabhatta — under Mihir Bhoja); development of art, sculpture and temple architecture; flourishing of learning centres in Kannauj, Kashi and Mathura

events.title: Defeat of Arab invaders
events.desc: Nagabhata I and Nagabhata II defeat Arab forces at the Rajasthan frontier, protecting North India from further Arab expansion.

events.title: Reign of Mihir Bhoja
events.desc: The greatest Pratihara ruler makes Kannauj the imperial capital and cultural heart of North India.

events.title: Decline of Pratihara power
events.desc: Internal weakness and the rise of the Chandellas, Kalachuris and Paramaras erode Pratihara control.

people.name: Nagabhata I
people.note: Defeated Arab invaders in Rajasthan.

people.name: Mihir Bhoja
people.note: r. c. 836–885 CE; capital at Kannauj; resisted Palas and Rashtrakutas.

people.name: Mahendrapala I
people.note: r. 885–915 CE; last powerful ruler of the early line.

prelims: Defenders of North India against Arab invasions; Kannauj was the imperial capital and cultural heart; strong administration with an efficient revenue system
mains: Gurjara-Pratiharas played a crucial role in protecting North India from foreign invasion; Kannauj became the greatest imperial and cultural centre of the age; they prepared the ground for later powers like the Gahadavalas in U.P.

quickFacts: Repelled Arab invasions; made Kannauj a great imperial centre
10th–11th century, due to internal weakness and rise of regional powers

periods.title: Kalachuris & Chandellas in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Regional Powers, Temple Culture, Political Decentralisation and Cultural Florescence
periods.overview: Both important regional powers of 9th–12th century North India, the Kalachuris and the Chandellas made Bundelkhand (Jejakabhukti, straddling present-day U.P. and Madhya Pradesh) their heartland. The Chandellas in particular are remembered for the world-famous Khajuraho temples, one of India's greatest architectural legacies.

phases.name: Rise of Regional Powers
points: Rise of regional powers in North India after decline of the Pratiharas; emergence of Kalachuris in Jejakabhukti (Bundelkhand region; parts of present U.P.)

phases.name: Rise of the Chandellas
points: Nannuka founds Chandella power; Yashovarman (925–950 CE) establishes independence from the Pratiharas

phases.name: Peak Power & Cultural Achievements
points: Period of greatest power and cultural achievements for both dynasties; Yuvarajadeva I of the Kalachuris (c. 915–945 CE) — titles Maharajadhiraja, Tribhuvanamalla, conquests in Bundelkhand; Dhangadeva and Gandharvavarman strengthen Chandella power

phases.name: Decline
points: Decline due to internal conflicts, attacks of Ghaznavids & Ghurids, and the rise of other powers; Vidyadhara (c. 1035–1050 CE) — greatest Chandella ruler, repelled Mahmud of Ghazni (c. 1022 CE) at Kalinjar, but the dynasty later declined

Administration & Governance: Kalachuris: monarchical rule with strong central authority, territories divided into provinces (Mandalas/Vishayas), officials (Mahasamantas, Uparika, Dandapashika), land revenue as the main source of income

Chandellas: well-organised administration, division into Bhuktis, Vishayas, Pattakas and Grams, officers — Vishayapati, Mahattaras, Dandadhikritas, Pustapalas; land revenue, tanks and wells were created; land grants to Brahmans, temples and officers
Society & Economy: Varna system continued; Brahmins and Kshatriyas enjoyed high status; growth of temple-based society; artisans, temple servants, dancers, musicians, traders flourished; women participated in religious and cultural life

Agriculture was the backbone; crops — rice, wheat, pulses, sugarcane, oilseeds; irrigation — tanks, wells, rivers, canals; trade & commerce flourished, use of coins; guilds (shrenis) of artisans and traders were active
Religion & Culture: Hinduism was the dominant religion (Shaivism, Vaishnavism, Shaktism, all flourished); Jainism also patronised by both dynasties; temples were centres of religion, art, education, economy and culture; temple architecture reached its zenith under the Chandellas

Art, architecture & literature: Khajuraho temples — world famous for Nagara style architecture; temples at Kalinjar, Mahoba, Ajaigarh, Deogarh etc.; fine sculptures, erotic art, mythological themes; use of sandstone; patronage of poets — Rajasekhara (under Mahendrapala of the Chandellas); development of music, dance and drama
Strengthened regional polity and administrative systems; patronised magnificent temple architecture (especially Khajuraho); promoted art, sculpture, literature and education; developed agriculture, irrigation and trade; U.P.'s Bundelkhand region became a great centre of culture and learning
Both dynasties contributed to political decentralisation but also cultural florescence in North India

events.title: Yashovarman establishes Chandella independence
events.desc: The Chandellas assert independence from the declining Pratiharas, beginning their rise as a major regional power.

events.title: Construction of the Khajuraho temples
events.desc: The Chandellas patronise the construction of the world-famous Khajuraho temple complex, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

events.title: Vidyadhara repels Mahmud of Ghazni
events.desc: The greatest Chandella ruler successfully defends Kalinjar against Mahmud of Ghazni's invasion.
