people.note: Founded Chandella power.

people.name: Yashovarman
people.note: r. 925–950 CE; established independence from the Pratiharas.

people.name: Vidyadhara
people.note: r. c. 1035–1050 CE; repelled Mahmud of Ghazni; patron of art & architecture.

people.name: Yuvarajadeva I
people.note: c. 915–945 CE; greatest Kalachuri ruler.

prelims: Kalachuris & Chandellas were important regional powers of 9th–12th century CE; their core area was Bundelkhand (Jejakabhukti), including parts of present U.P.; Khajuraho temples are a UNESCO World Heritage Site
mains: Both dynasties were great patrons of art, architecture, temples and culture; they contributed to political decentralisation but also cultural florescence in North India

quickFacts: Internal conflicts, Ghaznavid/Ghurid attacks, rise of the Gahadavalas

periods.title: Gahadavalas in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Regional Power, Cultural Renaissance, and the Last Major Hindu Dynasty in North India Before the Ghurid Invasions
periods.overview: The Gahadavalas, ruling from Kanyakubja (Kannauj) with Kashi and Prayaga as key centres, were the last great Hindu dynasty of North India before the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate. Their greatest ruler, Govindachandra, presided over a golden age of religion, learning and temple-building, before Jayachandra's defeat by Muhammad Ghori at Chandawar (1194 CE) opened the way for Turkish rule.

phases.name: Rise of Gahadavala Power
points: Rise of Gahadavala power in the Kashi region

phases.name: Chandradeva
points: Establishes the Gahadavala dynasty

phases.name: Expansion under Madachandra
points: Territorial expansion under Madachandra (c. 1030–1050 CE)

phases.name: Golden Age under Govindachandra
points: Greatest ruler; extended empire, promoted learning, religion & the arts; built temples, tanks & rest houses

phases.name: Decline & Defeat
points: Vijayachandra — last powerful ruler; 1194 CE: defeat of Jayachandra by Muhammad Ghori at Chandawar (near Etawah); early 13th century: decline and disintegration of the dynasty

Administration & Governance: Monarchical, hereditary kingship; empire divided into Bhuktis (provinces), Vishayas (districts) and Pattakas (sub-districts); officials — Uparika (governor), Vishayapati, Dandapashika, Mahattaras, Kayasthas and other officials

Land revenue was the main source; other taxes included trade tax, transit tax, fines and tributes; strong cavalry, infantry and elephants; king was supreme authority, Brahmanas consulted in judicial matters; maintained relations with neighbouring kingdoms, at times engaged in conflicts with Turko-Afghan invaders
Society & Economy: Varna system continued; Brahmanas enjoyed high status; growth of urban centres and market towns; artisans, traders, merchants and agriculturists formed important sections; women participated in religious, cultural and social life

Agriculture was the backbone of the economy; crops — rice, wheat, pulses, sugarcane, sesame; irrigation through tanks, wells, rivers and canals; active trade in local and long distance routes; land grants to Brahmanas, temples and scholars
Religion & Culture: Vaishnavism, Shaivism and Shaktism were prominent; King Govindachandra was a great patron of all religions; tolerance towards Buddhism and Jainism continued; confluence of religious traditions in Kashi and Prayaga

Flourishing of Sanskrit literature and learning; important scholar Vijnaneshvara (author of Mitakshara on Hindu law) under Govindachandra; development of temples, tanks, rest houses (Dharmashalas) and ghats; promotion of art, sculpture, music and dance
Temples built in Nagara style; major centres — Varanasi, Kannauj, Ayodhya, Ghazipur, Prayaga and surrounding areas; examples — Vishwanath Temple (Varanasi, earlier structures), Bhairav Temple (Kashi), Madan Mohan Temple (Kannauj) etc.; fine stone sculptures of deities, dvarapalas, surasundaris influenced by earlier Pratihara-Chandella traditions
Legacy & Importance: Gahadavalas were the last great Hindu dynasty in North India before the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate; promoted culture, learning, temples and urban development; strengthened Kashi and Prayaga as major religious and cultural centres; their period is important for understanding the transition from regional kingdoms to Sultanate rule

events.title: Chandradeva founds the Gahadavala dynasty
events.desc: Establishes Gahadavala control over Kashi and surrounding regions.

events.title: Reign of Govindachandra
events.desc: The dynasty's golden age: extended empire, promoted learning, religion and the arts, and built temples, tanks and rest houses.

events.title: Defeat of Jayachandra at Chandawar
events.desc: Muhammad Ghori defeats Jayachandra (Vijayachandra's successor) at Chandawar, near Etawah, marking the end of Gahadavala power and opening the way for the Delhi Sultanate.

people.name: Govindachandra
people.note: r. 1114–1154 CE; golden age of the dynasty.

people.name: Vijayachandra (Jayachandra)
people.note: r. c. 1170–1203 CE; defeated by Muhammad Ghori at Chandawar (1194 CE).

people.name: Vijnaneshvara
people.note: Author of Mitakshara, a landmark legal text, under Govindachandra.

prelims: Gahadavalas ruled c. 11th–12th century CE with capital at Kanyakubja (Kannauj); known for cultural revival, temples, literature and land grant system; defeated by Muhammad Ghori in 1194 CE
mains: Gahadavalas were the torchbearers of Hindu culture and the last line of defence against foreign invasions in North India; their period is important for understanding the transition from regional kingdoms to Sultanate rule

quickFacts: Defeat of Jayachandra by Muhammad Ghori, 1194 CE (Battle of Chandawar)

periods.title: Foundation of Cities in Medieval Period in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Urbanisation, Trade, Administration and Culture in Medieval Uttar Pradesh
periods.overview: A thematic study of how new cities were founded across medieval Uttar Pradesh — from Gurjara-Pratihara and Gahadavala towns through Delhi Sultanate garrison towns to Mughal imperial and administrative centres — and what factors, functions and characteristics drove medieval urbanisation in the region.

phases.name: Rise of Towns Under Regional Powers
points: Rise of important towns under Gurjara-Pratiharas and regional powers

phases.name: Growth Under Gahadavalas & Chandellas
points: Growth of religious, trade and administrative centres under the Gahadavalas and Chandellas

phases.name: Sultanate City Foundations
points: Establishment of new cities by Delhi Sultanate rulers for strategic and military considerations: Sambhal (founded by Shihabuddin Ghori's general, Kutubuddin Aibak's time, 13th c.), Badaun (Alauddin Khalji, 13th c.), Etawah (Khilji rulers, 13th c.), Ghaziabad (Ghazi-ud-din, 13th c.), Jaunpur (Malik Sarwar/Sharqi rulers, 14th c.)

phases.name: Mughal & Regional State Foundations
points: Foundation of cities under Mughals and regional states, cultural and economic flourishing: Fatehpur (Sikandar Lodi, 1482 CE), Agra (Sikandar Lodi, 1504 CE), Fatehpur Sikri (Akbar, 1571 CE), Allahabad (Akbar as Ilahabas, 1583 CE), Azamgarh (Akbar, 16th c.), Sikandra Rao (Akbar, 16th c.)

phases.name: Modern Transition
points: Modern cities emerge; colonial influence begins

Factors Behind Foundation of Cities: Strategic & military considerations (frontiers, defence); control over important trade routes; proximity to rivers, fertile land and markets

Administrative needs — provincial capitals, garrisons; religious & cultural centres attracted population; patronage of rulers, nobles, Sufis and merchants; growth of craft production and urban economy
Functions & Characteristics of Medieval: Administrative centres: provincial headquarters, court, revenue offices; military centres: fortress, garrisons, arsenals; economic hubs: trade, markets (bazaars), craft production
Cultural & religious centres: mosques, madrasas, temples, khanqahs, libraries; urban amenities: sarais, wells, tanks, bridges, roads, gardens
Economy & Urban Life: Active participation in regional and long-distance trade; products — textiles, metalware, ivory, pottery, leather, sugar, spices; guilds (shrenis), artisans, weavers, metalworkers, carpenters flourished; use of copper/silver coins, monetised economy; growth of moneylenders, merchants and bankers
Important trade routes: Delhi–Badaun–Kannauj–Jaunpur–Bengal; Delhi–Etawah–Gwalior–Central India; Agra–Allahabad–Varanasi–Bengal; Northwest (Punjab)–Sambhal–Ganga Plain
Administration of Cities: Shahna (Governor) or Iqtadars controlled the city and surrounding area; Muhtasib supervised markets, weights & measures, public morals; Kotwal maintained law & order; revenue collection through taxes on trade, land, houses and professions; strong fortification in many cities
Architectural & Cultural Heritage: Architectural features: fortresses, city walls & gates (e.g. Badaun, Jaunpur), mosques with arches, domes, minarets; sarais, bridges, tanks, gardens; blend of Indo-Islamic and local styles
Cultural contributions: Jaunpur — 'Shiraz-i-Hind' (centre of learning, music, literature); patronage of art, architecture, calligraphy, Persian literature; growth of Sufi centres and khanqahs

events.title: Jaunpur founded/rises as Sharqi capital
events.desc: Jaunpur emerges as one of medieval U.P.'s greatest centres of learning, music and literature — the 'Shiraz-i-Hind'.

events.title: Sikandar Lodi founds Agra
events.desc: Agra rises on the Yamuna, later becoming the imperial Mughal capital.

events.title: Akbar founds Fatehpur Sikri
events.desc: A planned city built as Akbar's capital for about 14 years.

events.title: Akbar founds Allahabad (Ilahabas)
events.desc: Built at the strategic confluence of the Ganga, Yamuna and Saraswati, becoming an important administrative and military centre.

people.name: Sikandar Lodi
people.note: Founded Agra (1504) and Fatehpur (1482).

people.name: Akbar
people.note: Founded Fatehpur Sikri (1571), Allahabad (1583), Azamgarh and Sikandra Rao.

prelims: Frequently asked in Prelims; important for Mains — development of urban centres, administration, economy, culture; link with trade routes, regional kingdoms, Delhi Sultanate & Mughal administration
mains: Cities act as engines of polity, economy and culture; U.P. was a major urban belt in Medieval India; many cities still exist today with historical legacy

quickFacts: Agra, Fatehpur, Fatehpur Sikri, Allahabad, Azamgarh
Laid the foundation for later urban growth in the colonial period

periods.title: Delhi Sultanate Period in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Establishment, Expansion and Administration of the Delhi Sultanate in U.P.
periods.overview: Uttar Pradesh was the core region of Delhi Sultanate power and administration across all five dynasties — Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi — with Sambhal, Badaun, Kannauj, Koil (Aligarh), Etawah, Varanasi, Chunar and Jaunpur all serving as major administrative, military, religious or cultural centres.

phases.name: Establishment
points: Establishment of the Delhi Sultanate by Qutb-ud-din Aibak

phases.name: Mamluk Consolidation
points: Iltutmish consolidates power in North India including U.P.

phases.name: Khalji Expansion
points: Alauddin Khalji conquers most of U.P.

phases.name: Tughlaq Rule
points: Administrative reforms; growth of towns

phases.name: Sayyid Decline
points: Decline of central authority; local chiefs grow in power

phases.name: Lodi Rule
points: Last Afghan dynasty before the Mughal invasion

Important Sultans and Their Connection w: Mamluk (Slave) Dynasty: Qutb-ud-din Aibak (1206–1210) laid the foundation of Sultanate power in U.P.; built mosques, consolidated control; Iltutmish (1211–1236) consolidated rule in North India including U.P.; Sambhal, Badaun developed
Khalji Dynasty: Jalal-ud-din Khalji (1290–1296) captured strategic forts in U.P.; Alauddin Khalji (1296–1316) conquered Awadh, Kannauj, Varanasi, Jalaun; introduced market reforms

Tughlaq Dynasty: Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq (1320–1325) strengthened administration in the Doab; Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1325–1351) undertook reforms, revenue measures, attempted capital shift, agricultural expansion; Firoz Shah Tughlaq (1351–1388) built canals in the Doab, developed cities, mosques, madrasas

Sayyid Dynasty: Khizr Khan (1414–1421) had weak control in U.P., local chiefs grew; Lodi Dynasty: Bahlul Lodi (1451–1489) reorganized administration in U.P.; Sikandar Lodi (1489–1517) developed Agra, encouraged agriculture, trade & arts; Ibrahim Lodi (1517–1526) defeated by Babur in 1526
Administration & Governance: Centralised Sultanate with the Sultan at the head; Iqta System — land revenue assignments to nobles in exchange for military service; provinces (Iqtas) headed by Iqtadars; strong revenue administration especially under Alauddin Khalji
Qazi, Muhtasib, Barid — important officials; development of a police & intelligence system; urban administration in major towns & cities
Society & Economy: Composite society: interaction of Turks, Afghans and local Hindus; growth of urban middle class — artisans, traders, soldiers, officials; emergence of new occupational groups — weavers, dyers, metal workers; Sufism played a unifying role; social mobility through service, trade & religious movements

Agriculture — mainstay; revenue improvement under Khaljis & Tughlaqs; canal construction (especially under Firoz Shah Tughlaq); growth of towns and trade centres — Kannauj, Varanasi, Koil, Sambhal, Badaun; development of crafts — textile, metal, pottery, leather, arms; active internal & external trade via land routes
Religion, Culture, Art & Architecture: Islam became dominant among the ruling class; construction of mosques, madrasas, tombs, khanqahs; Sufis — Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti (Ajmer, connected with U.P. travel), Nizamuddin Auliya visits the region; Hindi language & literature saw growth; Indo-Islamic architecture developed; cultural synthesis and syncretic traditions

Mosques: Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque (Sambhal), Adhai Din ka Jhonpra (influence in region); tombs: Tomb of Iltutmish (Delhi, influence), Sharqi & Lodi structures in Jaunpur; forts: Chunar Fort, Etawah, Kalpi; Persian was the official language; Hindi/Sanskrit literature continued; Amir Khusrau's cultural influence extended to the region
Legacy & Impact: Delhi Sultanate laid the foundation of political unification in North India; development of administration, revenue system and law & order; growth of cities, trade, crafts and agriculture; Indo-Islamic culture flourished in U.P.; Sufism promoted social harmony; prepared the ground for emergence of independent kingdoms (Jaunpur) and later the Mughals

events.title: Establishment of the Delhi Sultanate
events.desc: Qutb-ud-din Aibak founds the Delhi Sultanate, bringing U.P. under Turkish rule for the first time.

events.title: Alauddin Khalji conquers most of U.P.
events.desc: Awadh, Kannauj, Varanasi and Jalaun come under direct Khalji control, alongside major market reforms.

events.title: Firoz Shah Tughlaq's canals and cities
events.desc: Canal construction in the Doab and the development of new towns mark a period of infrastructure growth.

events.title: Defeat of Ibrahim Lodi
events.desc: Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat, ending the Delhi Sultanate's control over U.P. and beginning Mughal rule.

people.name: Qutb-ud-din Aibak
people.note: Laid the foundation of Sultanate power in U.P.

people.name: Alauddin Khalji
people.note: Conquered Awadh, Kannauj, Varanasi and Jalaun.

people.name: Muhammad bin Tughlaq
people.note: Undertook major reforms affecting the Doab region.

people.name: Sikandar Lodi
people.note: Developed Agra; encouraged agriculture, trade and arts.

prelims: U.P. was the core region of Delhi Sultanate power & administration; focus on cities — Sambhal, Badaun, Kannauj, Koil (Aligarh), Etawah, Varanasi, Chunar, Jaunpur; map-based questions on the Doab region, Ganga-Yamuna basin
mains: The Delhi Sultanate in Uttar Pradesh was not just a period of conquest, but of consolidation, administration and cultural synthesis that shaped the medieval history of North India

quickFacts: Doab (between Ganga-Yamuna), Awadh, Rohilkhand, Benares region
Defeat of Ibrahim Lodi by Babur, 1526 CE

periods.title: Jaunpur Sultanate in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: A Powerful Regional Sultanate that Made Jaunpur a Centre of Politics, Learning, Architecture and Indo-Islamic Culture
periods.overview: Emerging from the Sharqi governorship of Jaunpur under the declining Tughlaqs, the independent Jaunpur Sultanate — founded by Malik Sarwar in 1394 — became one of the most important regional powers of medieval North India, celebrated as a centre of learning and Indo-Islamic architecture (Atala Masjid, Lal Darwaza, Shahi Bridge) before its annexation by Bahlul Lodi in 1479.

phases.name: Foundation
points: Malik Sarwar (founder), the governor (nawab) of Jaunpur under the Tughlaqs, declares independence from Delhi

phases.name: Consolidation
points: Mubarak Shah (1398–1434) and Ibrahim Shah Sharqi (1434–1440) consolidate the Sharqi kingdom

phases.name: Peak & Cultural Flourishing
points: Mahmud Shah Sharqi (1440–1457) presides over Jaunpur's peak as a centre of politics, learning and architecture

phases.name: Decline & Annexation
points: Muhammad Shah Sharqi (1457–1479); constant wars with the Delhi Sultanate and Gujarat Sultanate weaken the kingdom; after the death of the last ruler, Jaunpur is annexed by Bahlul Lodi in 1479 CE, marking the end of the Sharqi dynasty

Administration: Sultan was the supreme authority; kingdom divided into parganas and villages; Iqta system prevailed; efficient revenue system based on land revenue
Officials: Diwan (finance), Ariz (military), Qazi (judicial), Kotwal (police chief); strong emphasis on law and order and public works
Military Power: Maintained a strong army with cavalry and infantry; fortified the capital Jaunpur; built forts and defensive structures; often in conflict with the Delhi Sultanate, Gujarat Sultanate and other neighbours
Society & Economy: Society was multi-religious and composite; Hindus and Muslims lived together, cultural synthesis developed; agriculture was the main occupation; development of irrigation and canals; trade and crafts flourished, with Jaunpur an important trade centre on the Ganga
Religion & Culture: Islam was the state religion; Sufism flourished with the presence of many Sufi saints; promotion of religious tolerance and coexistence; Persian was the court language; development of literature, poetry and music; Jaunpur became a great centre of learning and scholarship
Art & Architecture: Jaunpur style of architecture is distinct and grand; use of red sandstone and bricks; arches, domes, minarets and strong fortifications; blend of Islamic and local (Hindu) architectural elements

Major monuments: Atala Masjid — one of the largest mosques in Jaunpur; Jami Masjid; Lal Darwaza — famous for its grand gateway; Shahi Bridge (over the Gomti River); Jhanjhari Masjid; Maqbara of Malik Sarwar; Rampur Fort

events.title: Malik Sarwar declares Jaunpur's independence
events.desc: Founds the Sharqi dynasty and the independent Jaunpur Sultanate.

events.title: Mahmud Shah Sharqi's reign
events.desc: Jaunpur reaches its peak as a centre of politics, learning and grand Indo-Islamic architecture.

events.title: Annexation by Bahlul Lodi
events.desc: After the death of the last Sharqi ruler, the Jaunpur Sultanate is absorbed into the Lodi Sultanate.

people.name: Malik Sarwar
people.note: r. 1394–1398; declared independence from Delhi.

people.name: Ibrahim Shah Sharqi
people.note: r. 1434–1440; patron of learning.

people.name: Mahmud Shah Sharqi
people.note: r. 1440–1457; peak of Jaunpur's power and culture.

prelims: Founded in 1394 by Malik Sarwar; important rulers — Mubarak Shah, Mahmud Shah; Atala Masjid, Lal Darwaza, Shahi Bridge are important monuments; annexed by the Lodi dynasty in 1479 CE
mains: Jaunpur was not just a kingdom, it was a lamp of learning and culture in the medieval age of India; frequently asked in Prelims on rulers, monuments, dates; important for Mains on state formation, culture, architecture and regional powers of medieval India

quickFacts: 1479 CE, annexed by the Lodi Dynasty

periods.title: Delhi Sayyid & Lodi Dynasties in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Weaker Central Power Followed by Stronger Afghan Administration in U.P.
periods.overview: The Sayyids, founded by Khizr Khan after the decline of the Tughlaqs, held only weak control over Uttar Pradesh's nobles and provinces. The Lodis who followed — an Afghan (Pashtun) dynasty founded by Bahlul Lodi — built a stronger administration, with Sikandar Lodi in particular developing Agra and Sikandra as major cities, before Ibrahim Lodi's alienation of the nobles and defeat by Babur in 1526 ended Lodi rule.

phases.name: Sayyid Dynasty
points: Founded by Khizr Khan in 1414 CE; claimed descent from Prophet Muhammad (Sayyids); rose to power after the decline of the Tughlaqs; weak central power and challenges from nobles and regional rulers

phases.name: Lodi Dynasty Founded
points: Founded by Bahlul Lodi in 1451 CE; Afghan (Pashtun) dynasty; stronger administration than the Sayyids but faced noble opposition

phases.name: Lodi Consolidation
points: Sikandar Lodi's effective administration, coinage reforms, promotion of agriculture; built cities (Agra, Sikandra near Agra)

phases.name: End of Lodi Rule
points: Ibrahim Lodi alienated the nobles but was defeated by Babur at the First Battle of Panipat (1526 CE); ended the Lodi rule

Important Rulers: Sayyid Dynasty (1414–1451 CE): Khizr Khan (1414–1421) — consolidated Sayyid rule in Delhi and adjacent regions; Mubarak Shah (1421–1434) — coinage reforms, shift of capital within Delhi; Muhammad Shah (1434–1445); Alauddin Alam Shah (1445–1451)

Lodi Dynasty (1451–1526 CE): Bahlul Lodi (1451–1489) — centralised authority to a degree, laid foundation for stable administration; Sikandar Lodi (1489–1517) — effective administrator, promoted agriculture, built cities (Agra, Sikandra); Ibrahim Lodi (1517–1526) — alienated nobles, defeated by Babur
Administration & Governance: Central authority was weaker in the Sayyid period, improved under the Lodis; U.P. divided into Iqtas, governed by governors (muqtis); land revenue (kharaj) was the main source, with improved measurement under Sikandar Lodi
Army mainly Afghan cavalry with foot soldiers; Qazi courts and Sharia law, with Sikandar Lodi ensuring impartial justice; public works: construction of mosques, sarais, roads, tanks and gardens
Society & Economy: Afghans were the dominant nobility; agriculture was the backbone; use of iron plough, Persian wheel and better irrigation; growth of towns and markets; interaction between different communities continued; development of trade routes connecting Delhi–Agra–Jaunpur–Bengal; crafts like weaving, pottery, metal work flourished
Religion & Culture: Islam was the state religion; Sufism flourished, khanqahs established in many parts (Jaunpur, Delhi, Agra etc.); saints like Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti and Nizamuddin Auliya influenced the region

Use of Persian as the court language; development of literature, history writing and music; architecture saw continuance of Indo-Islamic style, including the development of Afghan-style architecture (arches, domes, thick walls, sloping buttresses)
Important buildings: Tomb of Khizr Khan — Delhi (early Sayyid); Sikandra (Agra) — built by Sikandar Lodi; Atala Masjid — Jaunpur (Lodi period); sarai buildings and forts in various towns
Sources: Tarikh-i-Mubarak Shahi (by Mubarak Shah's court), Tabaqat-i-Akbari (important for the Lodi period); coins — silver Tanka and copper Jital were in circulation

events.title: Khizr Khan founds the Sayyid Dynasty
events.desc: Establishes weak but formal control over Delhi and adjoining U.P. regions after the decline of the Tughlaqs.

events.title: Bahlul Lodi founds the Lodi Dynasty
events.desc: Begins a stronger Afghan administration in the region.

events.title: Sikandar Lodi's city-building programme
events.desc: Sikandar Lodi's administrative reforms and city foundations (Agra, Sikandra) mark the high point of Lodi rule in U.P.

events.title: Defeat of Ibrahim Lodi
events.desc: Babur's victory at the First Battle of Panipat ends Lodi rule over the region.

people.name: Sikandar Lodi
people.note: r. 1489–1517; effective administrator; built Agra & Sikandra.

people.name: Ibrahim Lodi
people.note: r. 1517–1526; defeated by Babur.

prelims: U.P. was a core region of the Delhi Sultanate under Sayyid & Lodi rulers; administration, revenue system and agriculture improved under the Lodis; the period witnessed growth of Indo-Islamic culture and Sufi influence
mains: Important for Prelims: rulers, dates, cities, administration, architecture; for Mains: analyse administrative measures, economic conditions, cultural developments and regional significance
'The Sayyids laid the foundation, the Lodis strengthened the structure, and the Mughals built the empire.'

quickFacts: Delhi, Agra, Sambhal, Etawah, Prayagraj, Ghazipur, Badaun

periods.title: Mughal Period in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: U.P. as the Political and Cultural Heartland of the Mughal Empire
periods.overview: Uttar Pradesh served as the political and cultural heartland of the Mughal Empire — the base for Mughal administration, economy, culture and architecture. Agra and Fatehpur Sikri served as imperial capitals, Allahabad and Kashi Vishwanath (Varanasi) were key administrative and cultural centres, and the region hosted the First Battle of Panipat (1526) and the Second Battle of Panipat (1556), as well as the construction of the Taj Mahal.

phases.name: Babur
points: First Battle of Panipat (1526) near Panipat (in present U.P. region's proximity)

phases.name: Humayun
points: Stayed in Agra; reorganisation of territories

phases.name: Akbar
points: Foundation of Fatehpur Sikri (1571); conquest & consolidation of Awadh; administrative reforms

phases.name: Jahangir
points: Allahabad (Prayagraj) becomes an important administrative centre; growth of trade and culture

phases.name: Shah Jahan
points: Construction of the Taj Mahal (Agra), Jama Masjid (Agra), Shahi bridges, gardens and sarais

phases.name: Aurangzeb
points: Long Deccan campaigns; administration continued from U.P. centres like Allahabad, Banaras

Administration & Governance: Territorial system: province of Subah (Sarkar); U.P. was part of Subah Allahabad and Subah Awadh; revenue system: Zabt system under Akbar, land revenue assessment through measurement (Todar Mal)

Mansabdari System: nobility system based on rank (Mansab) and salary; local administration: Pargana and Mahal system, Qanungos, Patwaris, Amin were important officials; law & order: Qazi (judicial) and Kotwal (police chief) maintained order in towns; public works: construction of roads, sarais, bridges, gardens, tanks and canals
Economy & Society: Agriculture was the backbone of the economy; main crops — wheat, rice, sugarcane, indigo; development of irrigation, use of Persian wheel and tanks; growth of trade and crafts — textiles, metal work, carpets, jewellery, pottery
Major trade centres: Agra, Banaras, Allahabad, Lucknow, Jaunpur, Etawah, Kannauj; society was composite — Hindus, Muslims, Jains, Sikhs lived together; local zamindars and merchants played key roles
Religion & Culture: Religious policy: Akbar followed Sulh-i-Kul (universal peace) and respected all religions; Jahangir and Shah Jahan continued a policy of tolerance; Aurangzeb was orthodox but allowed Hindu practices in various contexts

Cultural developments: flourishing of music (Tansen — linked with Akbar's court); miniature painting, calligraphy, silk weaving, carpet making; composite culture and syncretism of Indo-Islamic traditions; growth of the Sufi tradition, influenced by the Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti (Ajmer) connection
Art, Architecture & Literature: Architecture: Agra Fort (Akbar), Fatehpur Sikri (Akbar), Taj Mahal (Shah Jahan), Itimad-ud-Daulah's Tomb (Agra), Jama Masjid (Agra), Shahi Bridge (Allahabad), Shahi Qila (Allahabad Fort), gardens — Ram Bagh (Agra), Shalimar Bagh (Allahabad)
Literature: Akbarnama (Abul Fazl), Ain-i-Akbari, Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri (Jahangir), Padshahnama (Abdul Hamid Lahori); Persian was the court language
Important Mughal Rulers & Their Contribu: Akbar (1556–1605): conquered Awadh (1564), brought it under Mughal rule; founded Fatehpur Sikri (1571) near Agra; reorganised administration and revenue system
Jahangir (1605–1627): made Allahabad (Prayagraj) an important administrative centre; encouraged art and natural history
Shah Jahan (1628–1658): built the Taj Mahal, Jama Masjid (Agra), Moti Masjid; developed cities, gardens, sarais and roads
Aurangzeb (1658–1707): administered the empire from U.P. centres during Deccan campaigns; built many mosques and sarais

events.title: First Battle of Panipat
events.desc: Babur's victory establishes Mughal rule in North India, with lasting effects on the U.P. region.

events.title: Second Battle of Panipat
events.desc: Akbar defeats Hemu, consolidating Mughal control that will extend deeply into U.P.

events.title: Foundation of Fatehpur Sikri
events.desc: Akbar builds his new capital near Agra, a landmark of Mughal urban planning and architecture.

events.title: Construction of the Taj Mahal
events.desc: Shah Jahan builds the Taj Mahal at Agra, the defining monument of the Mughal period in U.P.

people.name: Akbar
people.note: r. 1556–1605; founded Fatehpur Sikri; conquered Awadh.

people.name: Jahangir
people.note: r. 1605–1627; developed Allahabad.

people.name: Shah Jahan
people.note: r. 1628–1658; built the Taj Mahal at Agra.

people.name: Aurangzeb
people.note: r. 1658–1707; administered the empire from U.P. centres.

prelims: U.P. was the core of the Mughal Empire — political, administrative and cultural; important rulers, dates, places, monuments, administrative systems (Sulh-i-Kul, Zabt system)
mains: The Mughals gave Uttar Pradesh political unity, economic prosperity and a rich cultural heritage that shaped its future; analyse impact on economy, society, culture, art, architecture and composite traditions

periods.title: Later Mughals in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Decline of Mughal Power & Rise of Regional Powers — Crucial for Understanding the Transition to Colonial Rule
periods.overview: Following Aurangzeb's death in 1707, Mughal power declined sharply and U.P.'s subahs became semi-autonomous under powerful Nawabs — chiefly the Nawabs of Awadh, whose capital Lucknow became the most powerful state in the region by the late 18th century. This period is crucial for understanding the transition from Mughal to Colonial rule.

phases.name: Onset of Decline
points: Death of Aurangzeb; decline of Mughal power begins; rise of regional powers, weak centre, administrative disintegration and foreign invasions

phases.name: Rapid Succession of Emperors
points: Bahadur Shah I (1707–1712), Jahandar Shah (1712–1713), Farrukhsiyar (1713–1719), Rafi-ud-Darajat (1719), Rafi-ud-Daula/Shah Jahan II (1719–1748), Ahmad Shah Bahadur (1748–1754), Alamgir II (1754–1759), Shah Alam II (1759–1806, nominal)

phases.name: Rise of Awadh's Nawabs
points: Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk (1722–1739) founds Awadh's autonomy; Safdar Jang (1739–1754) strengthens administration; Shuja-ud-Daula (1754–1775) defeated at the Battle of Buxar (1764); Asaf-ud-Daula (1775–1797) shifts the capital to Lucknow

phases.name: Colonial Encroachment
points: Diwani rights granted to the British by the Mughal Emperor (Allahabad Treaty, 1765); continued Awadh autonomy under Wajid Ali Shah's predecessors even as British influence grows

Administration & Governance: Weak central authority: emperors were figureheads, real power was with nobles, wazirs and regional governors; Subah system — U.P. was part of Subah Awadh and Subah Allahabad

Revenue system: Zabt system continued but revenue farming increased, with the Ijara system becoming common; Nawabs of Awadh (Saadat Khan, Safdar Jang, Shuja-ud-Daula, Asaf-ud-Daula, Wajid Ali Shah) became the de facto rulers; law and order deteriorated, zamindars became powerful in rural areas; Mughal army weak and undisciplined, reliance on provincial forces
Society & Economy: Agriculture remained the main occupation; irrigation through canals and wells; growth of commercial crops — indigo, opium, sugarcane; trade centres — Agra, Allahabad, Banaras, Shahjahanpur, Moradabad
Crafts and industries — textiles, metal work, pottery, glass, carpets, arms; society: influence of Persian culture continued, composite culture flourished
Religion & Culture: Islam remained the state religion, but tolerance continued; growth of Sufi centres — Chishti, Qadri orders; development of Urdu language; patronage to literature, music, painting (Mughal miniature style declined but provincial styles developed)
Important scholars: Shah Waliullah (born in Delhi, influence in the Awadh & Banaras region)
Art, Architecture & Literature: Architecture: blend of Mughal and regional styles; important monuments — Imambara, Rumi Darwaza (Lucknow), Asafi Imambara (Lucknow), Chhota Imambara, Dilkusha Kothi (Constantia, later colonial influence)

Literature & arts: Urdu poetry by Wali Dakhini, Mir Taqi Mir (Banaras connection); Persian literature continued; music and dance patronised at the Awadh court; painting declined in imperial centres but provincial schools like Awadh style flourished
Important Nawabs of Awadh (Impact on U.P: Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk (1722–1739): founder of Awadh's autonomy
Safdar Jang (1739–1754): strengthened administration, controlled U.P., Bihar
Shuja-ud-Daula (1754–1775): defeated Mughals & Marathas; participated in the Battle of Buxar (1764)
Asaf-ud-Daula (1775–1797): shifted capital to Lucknow, built many monuments
Wajid Ali Shah (1797–1856): last Nawab, deposed by the British in 1856; Awadh became the most powerful state in U.P. during the Later Mughal period

events.title: Death of Aurangzeb
events.desc: Marks the beginning of rapid Mughal decline and the disintegration of central authority across U.P.'s subahs.

events.title: Saadat Khan founds Awadh's autonomy
events.desc: Begins the rise of the Nawabs of Awadh as the de facto rulers of a major part of U.P.

events.title: Battle of Buxar
events.desc: Shuja-ud-Daula's defeat, alongside Mughal and Bengal forces, marks a decisive step toward British ascendancy in the region.

events.title: Diwani rights granted to the British
events.desc: The Allahabad Treaty grants the British East India Company revenue rights, deepening colonial encroachment on the region.

people.name: Shuja-ud-Daula
people.note: r. 1754–1775; defeated at the Battle of Buxar (1764).

people.name: Asaf-ud-Daula
people.note: r. 1775–1797; shifted the capital to Lucknow.

prelims: Later Mughals: 1707–1803 CE; important events: Nadir Shah's invasion (1739, impact on North India), Rise of independent Nawabs (1748 onwards), Battle of Plassey (1757), Battle of Buxar (1764, near Allahabad), Diwani rights granted to the British by the Mughal Emperor (Allahabad Treaty, 1765)
mains: 'With Aurangzeb died the power; what remained was only the shadow. Regional powers emerged where once stood the might of the Mughals.' This period is crucial for understanding the transition from Mughal to Colonial rule

quickFacts: Decline of Mughals & Rise of Regional Powers

periods.title: British Rule and Administration in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: A Mix of Exploitation and Modernisation — Laying the Base of Modern U.P.
periods.overview: From the Battle of Buxar (1764) that first brought British power to the region, through the formation of the North-Western Provinces (1835), the annexation of Oudh (1856), and their eventual merger into the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh (1902), British rule in Uttar Pradesh brought administrative centralisation, new land revenue systems, modern infrastructure, and English education — alongside heavy revenue demands, deindustrialisation and recurring famine.

phases.name: Early British Power
points: British power in U.P. began with the Battle of Buxar (1764); Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa granted to the East India Company in 1765; after the Regulating Act (1773), administration became more organised; Permanent Settlement introduced in some parts (not in U.P.) in 1793

phases.name: Formation of the North-Western Provinces
points: Charter Act (1833) — centralisation of administration; U.P. (then North-Western Provinces) officially formed in 1835; Lord William Bentinck reorganised territories; Agra and Allahabad Presidencies were merged; elite landlords and taluqdars given a share in administration

phases.name: Annexation of Oudh
points: Annexation of Oudh by Lord Dalhousie, a key grievance behind the 1857 revolt

phases.name: Consolidation & Reform
points: British rule brought administrative centralisation, revenue reforms, modern infrastructure, education and law & order systems; Local Boards Act (1884) introduced local self-government

phases.name: Bifurcation
points: The North-Western Provinces and Oudh were bifurcated into: (i) the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh, and (ii) Oudh (Chief Commissioner's Province)

Administrative Structure: Governor (Lieutenant Governor after 1858) — head of the province; Executive Council assisted the Governor; Commissioners headed divisions (Agra, Allahabad, Bareilly, Lucknow etc.)
District Collector — key officer, responsible for revenue, magisterial and administrative functions; Tehsil & Police System ensured law and order
Land Revenue Systems: Permanent Settlement: Western U.P. (Meerut, Saharanpur, parts of Muzaffarnagar); Mahalwari System: Rohilkhand, Agra, Bareilly, Allahabad etc.; Taluqdari System: Oudh region, where taluqdars collected revenue
Impact: heavy revenue demand, exploitation of peasants; rise of moneylenders and decline of the traditional rural economy; discontent among taluqdars, which played a role in the Revolt of 1857
Law, Order & Judicial System: Indian Penal Code (1860), Code of Criminal Procedure (1861) and Indian Evidence Act (1872) implemented; Police Act, 1861 introduced a modern police system; High Courts Act, 1861 — Allahabad High Court established (1866); Munsif Courts at the lower level for civil justice; British laws established a uniform system, but generally favoured colonial interests
Public Works, Education & Economic Impac: Development of roads, railways, canals, bridges, post and telegraph; first railway line in U.P. (1859, Allahabad to Kanpur); Grand Trunk Road improved; canals: Upper Ganga Canal (1842), Lower Ganga Canal (1854), Sharda Canal

English education promoted; schools & colleges established — Muir Central College Allahabad (1874), Agra College (1823), Isabella Thoburn College Lucknow (1870); universities — Allahabad University (1887), Agra College affiliated to it; emergence of social reform movements — Arya Samaj, Brahmo Samaj

Economic impact: expansion of commercial agriculture (indigo, opium, cotton, sugarcane); decline of handicrafts and traditional industries; drain of wealth — profits taken to Britain; famine and poverty (e.g. famines of 1837–38, 1860–61, 1873–74); rise of urban centres — Allahabad, Kanpur, Lucknow, Agra, Meerut
Local Self-Government & Freedom Movement: Local Boards Act, 1884 introduced local self-government — District Boards, Municipalities and Union Committees formed, though with limited powers and finances

U.P. was a major centre of nationalism — important leaders Pt. Madan Mohan Malaviya, Motilal Nehru, Jawaharlal Nehru, Chandra Shekhar Azad, Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqulla Khan; participation in Non-Cooperation (1920), Civil Disobedience (1930), Quit India (1942); revolutionary activities in Kanpur, Kakori (1925), Banaras, Allahabad

events.title: Battle of Buxar
events.desc: Establishes British political power in the region, leading to the grant of Diwani rights in 1765.

events.title: North-Western Provinces formed
events.desc: U.P. is officially organised as a distinct British administrative province.

events.title: Annexation of Oudh
events.desc: Lord Dalhousie's annexation of Oudh becomes a major grievance feeding into the Revolt of 1857.

events.title: Allahabad High Court established
events.desc: Becomes the apex judicial institution for the North-Western Provinces and Oudh.

events.title: Bifurcation into United Provinces
events.desc: The North-Western Provinces and Oudh are reorganised into the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh.

people.name: Lord William Bentinck
people.note: 1828–1835; reorganisation of the North-Western Provinces, administrative reforms.

people.name: Lord Dalhousie
people.note: Annexed Oudh in 1856.

people.name: Lord Canning
people.note: 1856–1862; annexation of Oudh, restructuring after 1857.

people.name: Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya
people.note: Prominent in U.P.'s freedom movement; founder of Banaras Hindu University (1916).

prelims: NWP & Oudh formed — 1835; bifurcation — 1902; Allahabad High Court — 1866; first railway line in U.P. — 1859 (Allahabad-Kanpur); U.P. important in the Revolt of 1857; key Acts — Police Act (1861), High Courts Act (1861), Local Boards Act (1884)
mains: British rule brought administrative centralisation but for colonial exploitation; land revenue systems caused rural distress and discontent; infrastructure and education laid the foundation for modern development; U.P. played a vital role in the freedom struggle

quickFacts: United Provinces of Agra and Oudh

periods.title: Revolt of 1857 in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: The First Major War of Independence — Widespread, Well-Organized and Led by People from Every Section of Society
periods.overview: Uttar Pradesh formed the strongest base of the Revolt of 1857, sparked at Meerut and spreading rapidly to Delhi, Lucknow, Kanpur, Jhansi, Bareilly and Allahabad. Led by figures like Nana Sahib, Begum Hazrat Mahal, Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah, Kunwar Singh and Khan Bahadur Khan, and drawing participation from soldiers, zamindars, taluqdars, peasants, artisans and common people alike, the revolt showed a genuinely mass, composite character before its suppression by 1858.

phases.name: Background & Outbreak
points: After the Doctrine of Lapse and annexations, British territories expand in U.P.; discontent among soldiers over low pay and the greased-cartridges controversy; harsh revenue policies affecting zamindars and taluqdars
10 May 1857: revolt at Meerut, sepoys march to Delhi; 11 May 1857: Bahadur Shah Zafar proclaimed Emperor at Delhi

phases.name: Spread Across U.P.
points: 30 May 1857: revolutionaries enter Lucknow; 5 June 1857: Allahabad captured by revolutionaries; 6 June 1857: Agra captured; 27 June 1857: Cawnpore (Kanpur) captured by Nana Sahib

phases.name: Resistance & Sieges
points: Strong resistance in Rohilkhand and Awadh; the British Residency at Lucknow besieged from July to November 1857

phases.name: British Reconquest
points: September 1857: British forces recapture Delhi; March 1858: British forces under Colin Campbell recapture Lucknow; by the end of 1858: organization of the revolt collapses after severe suppression

Nana Sahib (Neelkanth Peshwa) — Kanpur; led the revolt in Kanpur, proclaimed Peshwa
Begum Hazrat Mahal — Lucknow; led the resistance in Awadh in the name of her son Birjis Qadr
Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah (Faizabad) — Awadh region; popular religious leader who mobilised people
Kunwar Singh — operated in the Azamgarh–Ballia region, with links to Bihar; supported the revolt
Raja Jai Lal Singh — Aligarh; led the revolt in Aligarh
Khan Bahadur Khan — Bareilly; proclaimed himself ruler of Bareilly
The Revolt in Awadh (Lucknow & Faizabad): Awadh was the heartland of the revolt; Begum Hazrat Mahal took charge in the name of her minor son Birjis Qadr; Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah became the spiritual and military leader; people from all sections — taluqdars, peasants, artisans, women — participated; the British Residency in Lucknow was besieged from July to November 1857
Kanpur (Cawnpore) & Rohilkhand: Kanpur: led by Nana Sahib, Tatya Tope and Azimullah Khan; the British garrison surrendered on 27 June 1857; the Satichaura Ghat incident and the subsequent Bibighar incident took place; Kanpur was recaptured by the British in July 1857

Rohilkhand: widespread participation in Bareilly, Shahjahanpur, Budaun, Pilibhit, Moradabad, Rampur etc.; Khan Bahadur Khan proclaimed ruler of Bareilly; strong anti-British sentiments among Rohilla Pathans and local zamindars; the British regained control after heavy fighting
Nature, Significance & Reasons for Failu: Mass character in Awadh — involvement of peasants, taluqdars, clerics, artisans and women; combination of sepoy mutiny and a people's revolt aimed at ending British rule and restoring traditional authority; showed Hindu-Muslim unity (composite culture)

Reasons for failure: lack of centralised leadership and coordination; limited modern arms and ammunition; some princes and zamindars remained loyal to the British; better organisation, resources and communication of the British; internal differences among leaders
End of East India Company rule; Government of India Act, 1858; direct British Crown rule in India; policy of reconciliation with landlords and princes

Reorganisation of the army — more British, fewer Indians; strengthening of police, intelligence and communication; land settlements relaxed in Awadh to win support of taluqdars; beginning of modern nationalism

women.role: Leader of the revolt in Awadh
women.note: Took charge in the name of her minor son Birjis Qadr; led resistance at Lucknow.

events.title: Fall of Cawnpore (Kanpur)
events.desc: Nana Sahib's forces capture Kanpur after the British garrison surrenders; the Satichaura Ghat incident follows.

events.title: Siege of the Lucknow Residency
events.desc: British forces are besieged in Lucknow for months while Begum Hazrat Mahal leads resistance across Awadh.

events.title: Recapture of Lucknow
events.desc: British forces under Colin Campbell retake Lucknow, a major step in suppressing the revolt in U.P.

people.note: Proclaimed Peshwa; led the revolt in Kanpur.

people.name: Begum Hazrat Mahal

people.name: Khan Bahadur Khan

mains: It was a turning point in India's freedom struggle, leading to the end of Company rule and the beginning of Crown rule; use examples, data, timelines and maps in answers
Awadh was the soul of 1857 in Uttar Pradesh — it awakened the spirit of freedom that continued till 1947

quickFacts: Suppressed by 1858; Government of India Act, 1858

periods.title: Freedom Struggle in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: A Combination of Sacrifice, Leadership and Mass Participation Which Paved the Way for India's Freedom
periods.overview: Uttar Pradesh played a pivotal role in India's freedom struggle, from the very first spark of the 1857 revolt at Meerut through the rise of the Indian National Congress, the Swadeshi and Extremist phases, the Gandhian mass movements, and a vigorous parallel current of armed revolutionary activity centred on organisations like the Hindustan Republican Association and the Kakori Conspiracy. Nearly every phase of the all-India movement had a strong, often leading, U.P. chapter — from Motilal and Jawaharlal Nehru's Allahabad to the Kakori martyrs' Shahjahanpur and the Awadh Kisan Sabha's countryside.

phases.name: Early Resistance
points: First War of Independence; widespread uprising across U.P., centred on Meerut, Bareilly, Awadh, Jhansi, Kanpur and Fatehpur

phases.name: Rise of the National Movement
points: Indian National Congress formed (1885); socio-religious reforms and early political awakening across U.P.

phases.name: Swadeshi & Extremist Phase
points: Boycott, Swadeshi, national education, early revolutionary activities

phases.name: Gandhian Mass Movements
points: Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Quit India — genuine mass participation across the province

phases.name: Revolutionary & Parallel Activities
points: Armed revolutionary activities, secret organisations (HRA, HSRA), workers' and peasants' movements running throughout the period

phases.name: Final Phase
points: Quit India Movement, INA influence, the Naval Mutiny's effect, moving towards Independence

Major Centres of the Freedom Struggle in: Meerut — centre of the 1857 revolt; Kanpur — Nana Saheb, Tatya Tope; Lucknow — centre of politics, peasant movements; Allahabad (Prayagraj) — political activities, Congress sessions (1888, 1910, 1921); Ballia — 'first district to raise the tricolour', 1942
Revolutionary Movement: U.P. was a strong centre of revolutionary activities; important organisations — Hindustan Republican Association (HRA, founded by Ram Prasad Bismil and Sachindranath Sanyal) and Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA, Chandra Shekhar Azad)

Notable events: the Kakori Conspiracy (1925) — Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqullah Khan, Rajendra Lahiri, Roshan Singh etc.; Chandra Shekhar Azad's active base in Allahabad (Anand Bhavan); martyrs — Ram Prasad Bismil (Gonda), Ashfaqullah Khan (Shahjahanpur), Roshan Singh (Pratapgarh), Chandrashekhar Azad (Allahabad)
Peasant & Tribal Movements: Awadh Kisan Sabha (1920) — led by Baba Ramchandra; Eka Movement (1921) — Pratapgarh, against high rents, begar (forced labour), illegal cesses; Kisan Movements in Rae Bareli, Sultanpur, Faizabad, Gorakhpur, Ballia
Main demands: reduction in land revenue, abolition of begar, security of tenure; drew on Bardoli and Champaran-style methods and influences
Participation of Different Sections: Students: boycott of government schools, national education, students' unions active; Women: participation in movements, picketing, spinning, promoting khadi; Peasants: Kisan Sabhas, no-tax campaigns, agrarian agitations

Workers: railway, textile and municipal workers took part in strikes and protests; Business & Middle Class: boycott of foreign goods, Swadeshi, financial support; Religious & Social Leaders: promoted unity, social reform and national awakening
Important Institutions & Organisations: Indian National Congress Sessions — 1888, 1910, 1921 (Allahabad); Servants of the People Society — 1911 (Allahabad; Gokhale, Malaviya); Kashi Vidyapith — 1921 (Varanasi); Gandhi Ashram — 1921 (Allahabad); Awadh Kisan Sabha — 1920 (Awadh Region); Congress Seva Dal — 1923 (U.P. units active); Hindustan Republican Association (HRA) — 1924 (Shahjahanpur, Kanpur, Allahabad)

women.name: Women in the U.P. freedom struggle
women.note: Participated in movements, picketing, spinning and the promotion of khadi across the province.

periods.title: Socio-Religious Movements During Modern Age in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Reform, Rationalism, Education and the Awakening of National Consciousness in U.P.
periods.overview: The 19th and early 20th centuries witnessed a renaissance of thought across Uttar Pradesh, as British rule, Western education and Christian missionary activity triggered a wave of socio-religious movements — Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj, Ramakrishna Mission, Theosophical Society, the Aligarh Movement and the Sanatan Dharma Sabha — that worked for social reform, the removal of social evils, the spread of modern education, and the revival of ethical and spiritual values, laying the ideological foundation for U.P.'s role in the national movement.

phases.name: Background & Triggers
points: British rule, Western education and Christian missionary activities triggered socio-religious awakening; reformers sought to eradicate social evils and promote rationalism, education and social equality

phases.name: Brahmo Samaj in Kashi
points: Founded by Raja Shiv Prasad ('Sitare Hind') with the influence of Raja Rammohan Roy; opposed idol worship, caste system and social evils; advocated monotheism, women's education, widow remarriage and social equality

phases.name: Arya Samaj in Meerut
points: Founded by Swami Dayanand Saraswati; slogan 'Back to the Vedas'; opposed caste by birth, child marriage, idol worship, untouchability; promoted education, the Shuddhi movement, women's upliftment; established many DAV schools and colleges in U.P.

phases.name: Theosophical Society & Aligarh Movement
points: Theosophical Society (Allahabad, 1879) — founded by Madame H.P. Blavatsky with the support of Annie Besant; promoted universal brotherhood, study of religion and philosophy; Annie Besant established Central Hindu College, Varanasi (1898), which later became BHU

Aligarh Movement (Aligarh, 1875 onwards) — founded by Sir Syed Ahmad Khan; aimed at educational and social upliftment of Muslims; established the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College (1875), Aligarh; promoted modern education and social reforms

phases.name: Ramakrishna Mission & Sanatan Dharma Sabha
points: Sanatan Dharma Sabha (Varanasi, 1867) — founded to protect Hindu religion, cow protection and traditional values; opposed conversions and Christian missionary activities

Ramakrishna Mission (Varanasi, 1902) — inspired by the teachings of Ramakrishna Paramahansa and Swami Vivekananda; promoted Vedanta, universal brotherhood and service to humanity; established centres in Varanasi, Lucknow, Allahabad, Gorakhpur etc.

Raja Ram Mohan Roy (associated with Varanasi) — social reform, Brahmo ideas, women's rights, against Sati
Raja Shiv Prasad 'Sitare Hind' (Varanasi) — founder of Brahmo Samaj in Kashi, promoted education and widow remarriage
Swami Dayanand Saraswati (Meerut) — founder of Arya Samaj, social reform, Vedic revival, Shuddhi movement
Annie Besant (Allahabad) — educationist, social reformer, women's empowerment, founder of Central Hindu College
Sir Syed Ahmad Khan (Aligarh) — modern education, upliftment of Muslims, social reform
Pandita Ramabai (associated with Banaras) — advocated women's education and social welfare
Key Areas of Reform and Their Impact: Women's upliftment: Sati, child marriage, purdah and the devadasi system opposed; widow remarriage and women's education promoted
Caste system: opposed untouchability and caste discrimination; emphasized equality of all human beings
Education: establishment of schools, colleges and universities — DAV institutions, MAO College (Aligarh), BHU etc.
Religious reform: monotheism, return to scriptures, ethical religion and rejection of superstitions
Social unity: promoted communal harmony, national unity and moral values
Important Institutions Established: DAV Colleges & Schools (Series, 1886 onwards) — Arya Samaj (Swami Dayanand); Meerut, Kanpur, Varanasi, Agra etc.
Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College (1875) — Sir Syed Ahmad Khan; Aligarh
Central Hindu College (1898) — Annie Besant; Varanasi
Banaras Hindu University (BHU) (1916) — Madan Mohan Malaviya; Varanasi
Ramakrishna Mission Centres (1902 onwards) — Swami Vivekananda; Varanasi, Lucknow, Gorakhpur, Agra etc.
Significance, Connection with the Freedo: Laid the foundation for social reforms and the national movement; created awareness about rights, equality and education; built institutions that became centres of learning and nationalism; helped remove social evils and uplift marginalised sections

These movements awakened national political consciousness and a spirit of self-respect; leaders inspired by these reform movements actively participated in the freedom struggle; institutions like BHU, DAV colleges and the Aligarh Movement produced national leaders

Challenges: reforms were mainly urban and upper-caste centric; rural areas remained largely untouched; some movements were conservative in approach; women's participation was limited in the early phase

periods.title: United Provinces (U.P.) During Modern India
periods.tagline: United Provinces Was Not Just a British Administrative Unit; It Was a Land of Leaders, Movements and Sacrifices That Shaped Modern India
periods.overview: Formed on 1 April 1902 by merging the North-Western Provinces (NWP) with Oudh (annexed in 1856), the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh became one of British India's largest and most important provinces — politically, economically, administratively and culturally — with Allahabad as its capital and headquarters until 1920. Through the Morley-Minto and Montagu-Chelmsford reforms and, finally, provincial autonomy under the Government of India Act, 1935, the United Provinces built the administrative and political scaffolding that would carry directly into independent Uttar Pradesh.

phases.name: Formation
points: North-Western Provinces (NWP) + Oudh (annexed 1856) merge to form the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh (1902–1947); first Lieutenant Governor: Sir Antony MacDonnell (1902); headquarters at Allahabad

phases.name: Early Political Awakening
points: 1905: Partition of Bengal sparks strong reactions in U.P.; 1909: Morley-Minto Reforms — separate electorates, political awakening; 1916: Lucknow Pact — Congress & Muslim League unity at Lucknow; 1919: Jallianwala Bagh's influence, Rowlatt Act protests in U.P.

phases.name: Mass Movements
points: 1920–22: Non-Cooperation Movement — widespread participation; 1930–34: Civil Disobedience Movement — salt satyagraha, forest satyagraha (Terai), no-tax campaigns

phases.name: Provincial Autonomy & Quit India
points: Government of India Act, 1935 grants provincial autonomy; 1937 elections — Congress forms government under Govind Ballabh Pant; 1942: Quit India Movement — strong participation, parallel governments in some areas

Administration of United Provinces: Head of Province: Lieutenant Governor (appointed by the British Crown); Executive Council assisted the Lieutenant Governor; divisions (early 20th century) — Agra, Lucknow, Allahabad, Bareilly, Meerut, Benares, Gorakhpur etc.

District Administration: District Collector was the highest authority, responsible for revenue, magisterial and executive functions; Local Self Government: Municipalities (1884), District Boards (1884), Union Committees (1919 onwards); Judiciary: High Court established at Allahabad (1866), Munsif Courts for lower judiciary
Economy & Society: Agriculture was the main occupation; cash crops — indigo, sugarcane, opium; Land Revenue System — Mahalwari (majority), Taluqdari (in some Oudh areas); industries — handicrafts, textiles (Banaras silk), leather, sugar, glass (Firozabad), brass (Moradabad); railways expanded — Allahabad, Kanpur, Lucknow, Agra became major centres
Education, Press & Social Reforms: Education: Wood's Despatch (1854) impact continued; Universities Act (1904); Allahabad, Agra (now Dr. Bhimrao Ambedkar University), Banaras Hindu University (1916)

Press: rise of Hindi, Urdu, English newspapers — 'Leader' (Allahabad), 'Pratap' (Kanpur), 'Abhyudaya', 'Hindustan Times' (Delhi, impact in U.P.); Social Reforms: work of Arya Samaj, Brahmo Samaj, Theosophical Society, Ramakrishna Mission, Aligarh Movement (Muslim education)
Role of U.P. in the National Movement &: Strong participation in all phases of the freedom struggle; leaders emerged from U.P. who played an all-India role; U.P. became a base for revolutionary activities, Kisan movements and Congress politics; Awadh Kisan Sabha, Pratapgarh Kisan movement, Eka Movement based in U.P.

Major source of Congress leaders and workers; high participation in elections (1919, 1923, 1937); formation of Provincial Congress Committee (UP) — active in mobilisation; U.P. Legislative Council since 1935 — a platform for political debate; strong traditions of public meetings, sabhas, processions, prabhat pheris
Governance & Reforms (1919–1935): Government of India Act, 1919 — dyarchy introduced in U.P., limited self-government; Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms — transfer of some subjects (education, health, local self-government)
Government of India Act, 1935 — provincial autonomy, elections held in 1937 in U.P.; 1937 Elections — Congress formed government in U.P. (Pt. Govind Ballabh Pant, Premier)

periods.title: Formation of Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Uttar Pradesh Is Not Just a State, It Is a Legacy of History, a Centre of Culture, and a Strong Pillar of India's Unity and Progress
periods.overview: The state of Uttar Pradesh was not created in a single act, but emerged through nearly two centuries of administrative evolution — from the British-formed Province of Oudh (1775) through the North-Western Provinces (1835) and the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh (1902), to the renaming of the United Provinces as Uttar Pradesh on 24 January 1950 (with effect coinciding with India's new Constitution on 26 January 1950). Understanding this administrative genealogy is a recurring UPPSC theme, tying together British administrative history, the geography of the Ganga-Yamuna Doab, and U.P.'s central role in the freedom struggle.

phases.name: Formation of the Province of Oudh
points: The British establish the Province of Oudh under Company oversight

phases.name: Cession of Rohilkhand
points: Rohilkhand is ceded to the British by the Nawab of Oudh

phases.name: North-Western Provinces Formed
points: Created by Lord William Bentinck; included central Oudh region, Rohilkhand, Doab, Meerut, Saharanpur, Agra and Allahabad Divisions

phases.name: United Provinces of Agra & Oudh
points: Merger of the North-Western Provinces with Oudh; Chief Commissioner's Province; Allahabad made the capital

phases.name: Uttar Pradesh
points: 1947: U.P. becomes part of independent India; 1950: comes into existence as Uttar Pradesh with the Constitution, democracy and elected government, and the Indian Constitution became applicable

Key Factors in Formation: British administrative convenience and control; the need for efficient revenue collection and law & order; geographical contiguity and communication (roads, railways); socio-economic similarities of the regions; nationalist movements and the demand for self-governance
Oudh: Lucknow, Faizabad, Sultanpur, Rae Bareli, Barabanki, Sitapur, Hardoi, Unnao etc.; Rohilkhand: Bareilly, Moradabad, Bijnor, Rampur, Pilibhit, Shahjahanpur etc.

Doab (Upper Ganga-Yamuna): Meerut, Muzaffarnagar, Baghpat, Bulandshahr, Aligarh, Etah, Mainpuri, Farrukhabad etc.; Central Doab: Agra, Mathura, Hathras, Etawah; Allahabad Division: Allahabad (Prayagraj), Mirzapur, Jaunpur, Ghazipur, Basti, Deoria, Azamgarh, Ballia etc.; Bundelkhand (later addition): Jhansi, Lalitpur, Hamirpur, Banda, Fatehpur, Mahoba etc.
Role of Allahabad: Allahabad was the capital of the United Provinces (1902–1920); it was the political, administrative, educational and cultural centre; the Allahabad High Court of Judicature was established here in 1866; many important Congress sessions and political activities took place in Allahabad
Importance in the Freedom Struggle: U.P. was a hotbed of nationalist activities; many leaders like Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya, Pt. Motilal Nehru, Jawaharlal Nehru, Purushottam Das Tandon and Govind Ballabh Pant emerged from the region

Centres of movements included Allahabad, Kanpur, Varanasi, Lucknow, Gorakhpur, Bareilly etc.; Kisan movements — Awadh Kisan Sabha, Eka Movement; participation in Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience and Quit India Movements
From United Provinces to Uttar Pradesh: Name till 1949: United Provinces of Agra and Oudh; the Government of India Act, 1935 provided for provincial autonomy; post-1947, U.P. remained a part of independent India as a Chief Commissioner's/Governor's Province

On 26 January 1950, with the Constitution of India coming into force, it became a full State of the Indian Union under the official name Uttar Pradesh (U.P.), following the United Provinces (Alteration of Name) Order, 1950

periods.title: Political Developments in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: U.P. Has Not Only Witnessed India's Political Journey but Has Also Shaped the Destiny of the Nation Through Its People, Leaders and Movements
periods.overview: From the age of Mahajanapadas and Gana-Sanghas through the Delhi Sultanate, the Mughals and Later Mughals, Uttar Pradesh has been at the centre of Indian political history. In the modern period specifically, it moved from being the leadership base of the Indian National Congress during the freedom struggle, through decades of Congress dominance after Independence, to the post-1967 rise of regional and caste-based parties, the Mandal-era politics of the 1990s, and today's role as India's most politically consequential state — sending more members to the Lok Sabha than any other.

phases.name: Traditional Polities (Background)
points: Mahajanapadas, Gana-Sanghas, Delhi Sultanate, Mughals, Later Mughals — U.P.'s long political heritage before colonial rule

phases.name: The Revolt of 1857
points: Widespread participation in U.P. — Meerut, Kanpur, Awadh, Jhansi

phases.name: British Rule & Nationalist Rise
points: Formation of United Provinces (1902); rise of the Indian National Congress; mass movements

phases.name: Integration & Early Statehood
points: U.P. becomes part of independent India; Constituent Assembly and integration of princely states

phases.name: Congress Dominance & Reform
points: Congress dominance, land reforms, linguistic reorganisation, Panchayati Raj

phases.name: Rise of Regional Parties
points: Rise of regional parties, caste-based politics, the JP Movement, the Emergency

phases.name: Era of Identity Politics
points: Identity politics, coalition governments, governance reforms and developmental politics

Political Developments During the Freedo: U.P. was a stronghold of the Indian National Congress; important leaders — Motilal Nehru, Jawaharlal Nehru, Pt. Govind Ballabh Pant, Madan Mohan Malaviya, Purushottam Das Tandon, Acharya Narendra Dev; key movements — Non-Cooperation (1920), Civil Disobedience (1930), Quit India (1942)

Kisan movements — Awadh Kisan Sabha (Baba Ramchandra), Bardoli's influence, Eka Movement; active centres — Allahabad, Banaras, Lucknow, Kanpur, Gorakhpur, Faizabad; U.P. provided leadership, cadre and ideas for India's freedom struggle
Political Developments After Independenc: Formation of Uttar Pradesh (1950) — integration of various regions and princely states; dominance of the Indian National Congress under leaders like Govind Ballabh Pant, Sampurnanand, C. B. Gupta

Implementation of land reforms, zamindari abolition, community development programmes; linguistic reorganisation — formation of Uttarakhand (2000), Purvanchal & Bundelkhand (2011); political stability till the mid-1960s, later a multi-party era
Rise of Regional Parties & Political Soc: 1967 — decline of Congress dominance, rise of the Samyukta Vidhayak Dal; 1980s onwards — rise of caste-based regional parties; Mandal Commission recommendations (1990) — politics of OBC assertion; Kamandal politics — mobilisation on religious identity

Emergence of Bahujan politics — BSP under Kanshi Ram and Mayawati; Samajwadi Party (SP) founded in 1992 by Mulayam Singh Yadav; major parties: Indian National Congress, Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP), Samajwadi Party (SP), Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), Apna Dal (Soneylal)
Major Political Movements & Election Tre: Kisan Movements (1920s–1940s): Awadh Kisan Sabha, Eka Movement, Bardoli's influence; JP Movement (1974–75): Total Revolution movement led by Jayaprakash Narayan from U.P.; Anti-Emergency Movement (1975–77): U.P. was a major centre of opposition to the Emergency; Mandal Movement (1990): mobilisation for OBC reservation with major impact in U.P.; Dalit Movement (1980s–present): BSP's rise, focus on Dalit assertion & empowerment

Election trends: Congress dominance (1952–1962); Non-Congress wave and rise of SVD (1967); rise of BJP & regional parties (1989); caste-based politics dominates (1991–1996, SP-BSP rise); BJP strong phase (1998–2012); BJP landslide, clear majority (2017); BJP retains power (2022)
Role of U.P. in National Politics: U.P. has the highest number of Lok Sabha seats (80) — key to forming governments at the Centre; many national leaders have emerged from U.P. and shaped its politics; U.P. is a bellwether state, with political trends in U.P. influencing national outcomes; from nationalism to social justice to development — U.P.'s politics reflects India's changing priorities

periods.title: Reorganisation of Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: Reorganisation Is Not Just About Drawing Boundaries, but About Building a Better Future for Every Region and Every Citizen
periods.overview: Since its formation in 1950, Uttar Pradesh has been reorganised in phases reflecting India's linguistic reorganisation of states (1956), the long-standing hill-region demand that led to the creation of Uttarakhand (2000), the 2011 administrative division into Purvanchal and Bundelkhand for balanced regional development, and the creation of seven new districts and eighteen new tehsils in 2013 for administrative convenience — a continuing process that reflects India's dynamic federal structure and U.P.'s own regional aspirations.

phases.name: Formation of Uttar Pradesh
points: United Provinces becomes Uttar Pradesh on 26 January 1950

phases.name: States Reorganisation Act
points: Provides the basis of linguistic reorganisation of states nationally, consolidating U.P. as a large state

phases.name: Formation of Uttarakhand
points: Hill districts of U.P. carved out to form a new state (initially called Uttaranchal)

phases.name: Creation of Purvanchal and Bundelkhand Divisions
points: Administrative divisions created for balanced regional development

phases.name: New Districts & Tehsils
points: Internal administrative restructuring for better governance — 7 new districts and 18 new tehsils

Formation of Uttarakhand (2000): Long-standing demand of the people of the hill regions; reasons: difficult terrain and inaccessibility, neglect in development, distinct cultural identity, administrative convenience; carved out of 13 districts of U.P. (now Uttarakhand) on 9 November 2000
Districts carved out to form Uttarakhand: Almora, Bageshwar, Chamoli, Champawat, Dehradun, Haridwar, Nainital, Pauri Garhwal, Pithoragarh, Rudraprayag, Tehri Garhwal, Udham Singh Nagar, Uttarkashi
Creation of Purvanchal and Bundelkhand (: Announced on 20 August 2011 for balanced regional development; Purvanchal (Eastern U.P.): 21 districts; Bundelkhand (Southern U.P.): 7 districts; aimed at decentralised administration, faster development and better delivery of public services
New Districts Created in U.P. (2013): Seven new districts: Shamli (carved from Muzaffarnagar), Sant Kabir Nagar (from Sant Ravidas Nagar), Ambedkar Nagar (from Faizabad), Bhadohi (from Sant Ravidas Nagar & Varanasi), Chandauli (from Varanasi), Shravasti (from Bahraich), Siddharthnagar (from Maharajganj); 18 new tehsils were also created for better administration
Reasons for Reorganisation: Administrative Efficiency — to ensure effective governance and easy access to administration; Balanced Regional Development — to reduce regional disparities and promote inclusive growth; Linguistic & Cultural Identity — recognition of distinct linguistic, cultural and regional identities; People's Aspirations — fulfilment of long-pending demands; Better Delivery of Services — decentralisation for faster and better public service delivery
Impact of Reorganisation: Improved administration and governance; focused development of backward regions; strengthened regional identity and cultural pride; better infrastructure and connectivity
However, challenges remain: regional disparities, resources sharing, and border issues between the reorganised units

periods.title: Economical and Social Progress in Uttar Pradesh
periods.tagline: The Progress of Uttar Pradesh Is the Progress of New India — Balanced Economic Growth and Social Justice Are the True Pillars of a Developed U.P.
periods.overview: As India's most populous state, Uttar Pradesh has made significant progress in economic development and social advancement since Independence, underpinned by a large agricultural base, a vast workforce, and growing industrial and infrastructural investment. It ranks 2nd nationally in GSDP with a highest-in-India workforce, yet continues to close persistent gaps in literacy, female literacy, and health indicators relative to the national average — making balanced regional development between resource-rich western/central U.P. and lagging Purvanchal/Bundelkhand a central policy priority.

phases.name: Economic Overview
points: GSDP (Nominal): approx. ₹24.89 lakh crore, 2nd in India; share in India's GSDP: approx. 8.3%; per capita income (2022–23): approx. ₹57,033, below the national average
Workforce (2023): 10.2 crore+, the highest of any state; contribution to FDI inflow (2000–2023): approx. 5%, among the top 5 states; Ease of Doing Business Rank 2020: 2nd

phases.name: Agricultural & Industrial Base
points: Largest producer of foodgrains in India; highest sugarcane production; leading state in milk production; success of the 'Mukhya Mantri Krishi Sinchai Yojana', crop diversification, soil health mission

U.P. is an emerging industrial hub of North India — textiles, leather, handicrafts, brassware, glassware, sports goods, food processing, IT/ITeS; Noida, Greater Noida, Yamuna Expressway Industrial Development Authority (YEIDA) are major industrial growth engines; One District One Product (ODOP) initiative promotes local products globally

phases.name: Investment & Infrastructure
points: 'UP Investors Summit' has attracted large investments and MoUs; industrial corridors — DMIC influence, Bundelkhand Industrial Development Authority; Film City (Noida), Toy City (Greater Noida), Electronics Manufacturing Policy

Infrastructure: Purvanchal Expressway, Bundelkhand Expressway, Ganga Expressway, four-laning of rural roads; Dedicated Freight Corridor, Vande Bharat trains, station modernisation; Jewar Airport (Noida), Kushinagar, Ayodhya, Gorakhpur, Chitrakoot Airports; Smart Cities — Lucknow, Kanpur, Varanasi, Agra, Prayagraj

phases.name: Social Development
points: Literacy rate (15+ years): 67.7% in U.P. vs 77.7% nationally; female literacy rate: 59.4% vs 70.3% nationally; school enrolment (6–14 years): 97.1% vs 96.5% nationally

Institutional delivery: 79.8% vs 88.6% nationally; Infant Mortality Rate: 37 per 1000 live births vs 28 nationally; Maternal Mortality Ratio: 155 per lakh live births vs 97 nationally; stunting in children under 5: 43.1% vs 35.5% nationally

Education and Human Development: Expansion of basic education infrastructure — schools, colleges, universities; launch of Kanya Vidya Dhan, Mission Shakti, Beti Bachao Beti Padhao; new universities — BBAU, Central University of South Asia, Mahatma Gandhi Kashi Vidyapith (Central University); skill development through the Kaushal Vikas Mission; improvement in digital education and e-governance in schools
Health and Nutrition: Expansion of healthcare facilities — PHCs, CHCs, district hospitals, medical colleges; Ayushman Bharat covers a large number of beneficiaries; Mission Indradhanush, Nikshay Mitra, TB control programmes; nutritional support through ICDS, POSHAN Abhiyaan, mid-day meal scheme
Social Welfare and Inclusion: Reservation policies for SCs, STs, OBCs and EWS; welfare schemes — Old Age Pension, Widow Pension, Divyang Pension; Housing for All, Ujjwala Yojana, PM Awas Yojana; free ration under NFSA, health insurance; upliftment of weaker sections and empowerment of women through self-help groups; promotion of minority welfare and inclusive development
Poverty Alleviation, Employment & Women': Decline in the poverty ratio over the decades; MGNREGA — rural employment and asset creation; self-employment schemes — PMEGP, ODOP, MUDRA loans; growth in the service sector and urban employment

Mission Shakti — women's safety, security and empowerment; increase in women's SHGs and financial inclusion; 33% reservation in Panchayati Raj Institutions; Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana, Matru Vandana Yojana; more women's participation in education, workforce and entrepreneurship
Culture, Tourism, Heritage & Challenges: Rich cultural heritage — Varanasi, Ayodhya, Mathura, Sarnath, Kushinagar, Prayagraj, Dudhwa; promotion of spiritual, eco and heritage tourism; Kumbh Mela, Dev Deepawali, Ramayana Circuit boosting the economy; conservation of monuments and promotion of local arts and handicrafts

Challenges: regional imbalance — Purvanchal and Bundelkhand lag behind; low per capita income and industrialisation in some regions; unemployment and underemployment; low literacy and health indicators compared to the national average; population pressure, urban congestion, pollution and environmental degradation

women.note: Growth in women's SHGs, financial inclusion, and entrepreneurship under Mission Shakti and related schemes.
